A new positioning technology could make autonomous vehicles and robotaxis more reliable at recharging themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers in Japan have developed a new technology that could enable electric vehicles (EVs) to charge "simply by parking".

Wireless charging is still relatively nascent in the EV market, but scientists hope that integrating more wireless charging devices into roads and parking spaces will move the EV industry away from bulky plug-in infrastructure. It uses the same wireless power transfer technology found in modern smartphones and consumer electronics: a transmitter coil inside in a ground pad generates an oscillating magnetic field, which induces an electric current in a receiver coil underneath the vehicle. This current recharges the EV's battery cells.

However, small misalignments between the two coils can affect how quickly and efficiently the battery recharges. This new system uses short-range radio signals to determine the position of the vehicle's magnetic charging coil relative to the charging device in the ground, including its distance and angle. This helps the EV and its driver get into the optimal position for efficient charging.

The technology could be particularly useful for driverless "robotaxis" and other autonomous vehicles that need to be able to recharge quickly and efficiently without human assistance, the researchers said. They detailed their findings in a study published Aug. 26 in the IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology.

"We hope this research will lead to a future where EVs charge simply by parking, much like smartphones placed on wireless chargers," Ryotaro Hada, first author of the study and a master's student at the University of Osaka's Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, said in a statement.

Existing methods for aligning an EV's charging coil with a wireless charging pad use magnetic sensors or cameras. Magnetic systems work best when the coil is close to the pad, while cameras can struggle in rain, poor lighting or when dirt obscures the pad, the researchers explained.

This new system uses four ultra-wideband radio devices mounted around the vehicle's charging coil to communicate with four antennas around the charging pad.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By measuring how long radio waves take to travel between the ultra-wideband devices and the antennas, as well as detecting tiny differences in how the signals arrive at each of the vehicle's sensors, the system can pinpoint the position and angle of the EV's charging coil relative to the ground pad.

The same technology is used in some digital car keys. They use short radio pulses to detect when the driver is close by, allowing the driver to unlock their vehicle without requiring a physical key.

In laboratory experiments using a scaled-down vehicle model, the system worked out where the vehicle's charging coil was to within 0.09 inches (2.32 millimeters) of its actual position and which direction it was facing to within 0.25 degrees. Correcting for distortions in the radio signals reduced the positioning error by around fivefold, the team said.

The researchers noted that the system still needs to be tested outdoors, on full-size EVs and under real charging conditions.

#6310. Foster bill would bolster tech use to monitor AI financial risks

"We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector," said Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

A leading Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee introduced legislation Thursday aimed at helping regulators use technology to better spot financial stress turbocharged by artificial intelligence and around-the-clock payment systems.

The draft bill, from Rep. Bill Foster, D-Ill., would require the Federal Reserve to work with other regulators to develop, test and publicly release model software that would improve the ability to assess market conditions in real time and respond quickly to cybersecurity and other threats.

The bill is designed to help regulators keep pace with new risks "driven largely by the development of state-of-the-art AI models," according to a summary.

The legislation is intended to help regulators provide financing to banks during crises and wind down failing banks. The model software would reduce the amount of manual compliance work that smaller financial institutions would have to do by providing standard data formats for regulatory reporting and tools to manage and transmit the information to regulators, according to a Foster spokesperson.

“With advances in AI creating new cybersecurity threats and financial risks, it's more important than ever that we modernize the way we monitor the health of our financial institutions,” Foster said in a statement. “We cannot afford to rely on outdated systems to oversee an increasingly complex financial sector.”

Foster, who has a Ph.D. in physics and has been a leader on AI issues on the Financial Services panel, is in line to become chair of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee next year.

He has been mulling a challenge to ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., to chair the full committee in the new Congress. But Foster is now “leaning toward not running,” a person familiar with his thinking said.

Waters already has a confirmed challenger in Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., who on Thursday circulated a "Dear Colleague" letter seeking the support of House Democrats for his bid.

Casten touted his “career at the intersection of business, science and public policy." Before entering Congress, he worked in clean energy and co-founded a company that converted industrial waste energy into usable power.

In his letter, Casten cited the need to lower housing and insurance costs, protect consumers from fraud, address risks posed by cryptocurrency and prediction markets and guard against the next financial crisis. He also promised to hold the Trump administration accountable for ethical lapses.

He's got a tough road ahead of him, however. Every Financial Services Democrat except Casten, Foster and Rep. Sam Liccardo of California signed an Oct. 21 letter to House Democrats in support of Waters. That show of support came after Casten made it known he was interested and it was clear that Foster had been considering his own bid.

Although Foster may not compete for the chairmanship, he has recently talked to Waters about changing how the committee operates.

“He wants a variety of members to play a role in legislation brought up in committee,” the source familiar with his thinking said. He’s also seeking more input on witnesses who testify at subcommittee hearings.

The draft bill he released on Thursday covers a topic that Foster is likely to pursue throughout the 120th Congress. He often asks the most questions about the use of AI in financial services at hearings and offers the most amendments related to the issue at markups.

Under the bill, model software would be developed for banking records and operations, regulatory reporting, stress testing, anti-money laundering and fraud screening, AI risk monitoring and other activities.

The software must be open source, publicly available and tested for reliability and accuracy, according to the summary. It would be tested using synthetic or legally permitted historical data rather than actual customer accounts. Regulators would not take financial or supervisory actions during the study.

The software developed during the study would not have to be adopted; rather, it “should be viewed as a starting point for further modernization,” the summary says.

All software models would have to be published within one year of enactment of the bill and a final report assessing feasibility, costs and savings, competition and other criteria, would be due to Congress within two years.

#6309. Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.

Diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count. A new study suggests that one of the best ways to follow them may be through a tiny flatworm that lives in their intestines and in the snails they eat.

By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.

They also found a genetic dividing line about 300 kilometers south of where turtle experts had drawn the boundary between two terrapin subspecies.

The study was carried out by researchers from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute and East Carolina University.

The diamondback terrapin is the only North American turtle that lives exclusively in brackish water, in salt marshes and estuaries along the coast. For a long time, people mostly ate it.

Turtle soup was a fashionable dish, and hunting for it drove the species into steep decline until the early 20th century. Then, in 1920, Prohibition banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes.

Demand collapsed, and so did the hunting.

That wasn’t a happy ending, though. Terrapins kept declining because of habitat loss, coastal development, and drowning in crab pots.

The species is now listed as “vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List. Conservationists want better data on where terrapin populations live and how they’re connected.

But the turtles are secretive and spread out, and catching enough to answer those questions is slow, expensive work.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. It can’t complete its life without two hosts.

Its eggs pass out in terrapin droppings and are eaten by eastern mudsnails. Inside the snail, the fluke multiplies by cloning itself.

Its larvae then leave the snail’s soft body and form small pearly cysts on the hard plate the snail uses to seal its shell.

When a terrapin eats an infected snail, the fluke grows into an adult in the turtle’s gut and reproduces sexually there.

This arrangement is what makes the fluke useful. Mudsnails are abundant and easy to collect, and they barely move.

Terrapins are the ones that carry the parasite from marsh to marsh. If the turtles don’t travel, the fluke’s genes don’t travel either. In principle, the parasite’s family tree should trace the turtle’s movements.

“One of the biggest challenges in conserving vulnerable species is understanding how populations are distributed and connected without having to capture and handle large numbers of animals,” said senior author Michael McCoy from FAU Harbor Branch.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an important window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins.”

The team collected mudsnails from Cape Cod in Massachusetts to St. Augustine in Florida and dissected more than 4,000 of them. Infections inside the snails were rare, never reaching 4% at any site.

The cysts outside were far more common, appearing on as many as 74% of snails at some marshes. Altogether, the fluke turned up at 23 of the 29 marshes sampled.

Finds on Cape Cod and in northeast Florida pushed its known range further north and south.

The Wetlands Institute provided the researchers with 38 female terrapins that had been killed by cars in New Jersey.

Seventeen of them carried adult flukes, with up to seven worms per turtle.

From 476 genetic sequences, the team found 102 distinct versions of a stretch of the fluke’s mitochondrial DNA. More than three-quarters of these versions turned up at only one location.

One version dominated the northern marshes, and another dominated the south. The farther apart two marshes were, the more their flukes differed genetically.

That fits what is known about terrapins. The most mobile of them, adult females, have been recorded traveling no more than 8.5 kilometers. If the hosts stay close to home, their parasites become local too.

The most striking result was where the sharpest split fell. Biologists have traditionally drawn the line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin at Cape Hatteras in North Carolina.

The fluke’s genetic break falls instead between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina, near the state border. That’s about 300 kilometers further south.

Terrapin subspecies were originally defined by their appearance, before genetic tools existed, so the parasite’s data adds to growing questions about where the real boundaries lie.

The study also turned up something nobody had described before. Most fluke cysts are pearly white, but some had a faint blush or a pink ring around the edge, while others were bright fuchsia.

They first appeared in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and New Jersey, sometimes on the same snail as ordinary cysts. The color is in the cyst wall, not in the larva inside.

The pink cysts didn’t match any genetic group, and the researchers don’t yet know what causes them. One possibility is that they are simply older.

The authors make a broader point. Parasites account for nearly half of all known species, yet they are rarely studied and almost never protected.

When a host declines, its parasites decline with it. Scientists recently formed an IUCN group dedicated to parasite conservation, and this study adds basic range and diversity data for a parasite that has been almost entirely ignored.

The team is careful not to overstate the results. The analysis used a single genetic marker, which is inherited only through the mother.

No one has yet compared fluke genetics directly with terrapin genetics from the same marshes, and that test will decide whether the fluke truly mirrors its host.

Counting cysts is also not a straightforward way to count turtles. One earlier study found that cyst numbers explained less than 8% of the variation in terrapin abundance.

“Our results point to an opportunity to look at conservation from a different perspective,” McCoy said.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them.”

“Understanding where these parasites occur and how their populations are genetically connected could help scientists identify important geographic divisions and develop better questions about how terrapin populations should be monitored and managed.”

The study is published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

#6308. The 8 Best Pet Hair Vacuums Designed for Homes That Never Stop Shedding

We evaluated models from top brands including Dyson, Bissell, and Shark.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Getting pet hair out of carpets and off of tile and hardwood is a constant battle many are familiar with, and trying to remove those persistent hairs that have embedded themselves into your upholstery is another beast. Choosing the right vacuum can significantly improve your cleaning routine if you’re a cat or canine parent.

The top pet hair vacuums are designed with powerful suction and superior filtration (plus, they come with special attachments) to capture fine hair, thick fur, and pet dander. Regardless of whether you have a fluffy cat, a long-haired pup, or both, investing in a vacuum specifically made for pets will help you keep messes in check for a tidier home.

Upright and canister vacuums are the strongest options for deep cleaning, but cordless stick vacuums, handheld vacuums, and robot vacuums all aid in daily pet hair control. Units that have tangle-free brush rolls and easy-to-empty dustbins are best for reduced maintenance, and a HEPA filter is essential for clearing out dust and dander that may trigger your allergies.

I researched and hands-on-tested lots of vacuums to find versions that truly pick up pet hair, focusing on features, bin capacity, and filtration. Below are my choices, as well as advice and important pointers to consider before you shop.

I initially considered a range of vacuum styles, from uprights to robots to canisters. Keeping in mind different price points, I chose models that provide an optimal combination of suction strength, versatility, pet-focused features and tools, and value.

I tested the Shark AZ2002 Vertex in a home with two American Shorthair cats, three different floor types, and multiple area rugs. I cleaned everything from tracked litter and dust on laminate and carpet to pet hair on furniture and upholstery, trying out the different suction power modes and attachments as I went. I vetted the features that I thought would be most helpful for animal owners such as HEPA filtration, a motorized pet tool, and an anti-tangle brush roll. Based on this research and testing, these are my top recommendations for the best pet hair vacuums.

One of the things I liked most about this upright model is its specially crafted vacuum head, which uses both a soft roller brush and paddled, fin-like brush roll to pick up embedded hair, fine dust, and dirt from all types of flooring. I noticed that this method prevents longer hair from getting tangled in the brush roll and allows for a deeper clean overall.

Cleaning modes are easy to access with a simple switch on the handle, and the vacuum head has LED lights that illuminate hidden dust bunnies and stray pet hair, which was extremely helpful when cleaning under furniture and in corners.

Another major plus is that this upright model also converts into a motorized, lift-away pod for cleaning other surfaces like couch cushions and stairs. The vacuum’s hose stretches up to an impressive 12 feet, and it comes with a crevice tool and pet upholstery tool. I tried the motorized pet tool on polyester couch cushions, and it didn’t struggle to pick up embedded pet hair.

The Vertex has a large, 1-quart dustbin to accommodate more hair, along with a fully sealed HEPA filtration system to capture pet dander. And while it’s heavy, it navigates pretty easily.

Full Shark AZ2002 Vertex Upright Vacuum Review

It’s hard to come by a vacuum that is less than $200 that doesn’t skimp on suction power, assets, or reliability. This model offers all of the above at an accessible price. Our tester has been using this vacuum for four years and has yet to be disappointed.

“This vacuum has a brush roll with multiple rows of bristles that kick out any hair that’s really deep inside a variety of fibers, including rugs and carpets.”

It works just as well on hardwood floors, and the swivel-steering vacuum head is easy to maneuver under and around furniture. The power cord is extremely long, extending 27 feet, and is automatically retractable with the cord rewind mechanism.

The CleanView comes with attachments for removing pet hair from stairs and hard-to-reach corners on hardwood and carpeted floors. It’s easy to empty, too, with a button on the front that releases dirt directly into the garbage.

One main complaint from our tester is that, given the size and weight of this upright model, it can be a pain to shuffle around as you clean. “Dragging around the Cleanview to different rooms of the house requires some effort. The vacuum weighs 15 pounds, which doesn’t seem like a lot until you need to get to a different part of your home.”

Full Bissell Cleanview Swivel Rewind Upright Vacuum Review

Dyson is most recognized for its powerful vacuums, and if you’re on the hunt for a machine that easily pulls pet hair out of your shaggiest of carpets, you won’t be disappointed with the Ball Animal 3 Extra model.

Besides strong suction, this vacuum boasts a five-layer, complete filtration system that captures dust and pet dander, preventing them from being released back into the air. The floor head has an integrated comb that untangles hair from the brush roll as it rotates, keeping lengthy strands from getting ensnared.

The vacuum is simple to handle thanks to the brand’s distinctive ball design, and it includes a combination tool, stair tool, turbine tool, and a pet groom tool. The wand is instant-release and has an extended hose for reaching isolated areas like underneath your couch or around dining room chairs.

This powerful vacuum has a sealed HEPA filtration system to securely trap dirt, dander, and fur so they don’t recirculate back into your home as you clean. It works on a variety of surfaces but handles hardwood floors the best because its good suction control prevents larger debris from scattering.

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser also has a tangle-free brush roll, and even after using the vacuum on two large area rugs and hardwood floors for months, I haven’t had to cut any hair from the bristles. Plenty of cat fur, dirt, and dander makes its way into the dustbin as the suction power is strong enough to agitate carpet fibers and pick up debris that might not be completely visible.

I love that there is a dedicated pet hair attachment for the hose wand. It works well on couch cushions, and a few pushes back and forth removed a majority of the mess. Plus, the vacuum converts into a canister pod, so it moves around easily as you work around your space.

The convertible design adds maneuverability, and the attachments included are helpful for more precise cleaning.

Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Full Review

The Bissell Pet Hair DualBrush packs two brush roll types into one vacuum. The first loosens and cleans debris that’s stuck to your floor or caught up in carpet fibers, and behind it, a second brush roll makes closer contact with the floor to pick up the now loosened debris. Powerful suction delivers strong pet hair pickup, too.

This model converts to a handheld-style canister vacuum that lifts off of the base, so you can easily clean hard-to-reach areas or furniture. We appreciate that this design also has LED lights on the vacuum floorhead and pet hair attachment to illuminate hidden dust and debris.

The DualBrush uses sensors to automatically detect the level of dirt and dust on the floor, and will adjust suction power accordingly, helping you get a deeper clean in situations where it’s most needed. It weighs 17 pounds, which may be a pain to push around for longer cleaning sessions, but that isn’t uncommon for an upright vacuum.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser DualBrush Upright Vacuum Review

The Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo comes with multiple features that are a standout for pet owners. This model is equipped with a HEPA filter to keep allergens out of your home, and the canister detaches from the base, making it easier to clean stairs, around baseboards, and along blinds. Just keep in mind that the hose only extends seven feet, so you’ll have to carry the detachable pod close by.

Some noteworthy attachments are a tangle-free brush roll and a motorized tool that’s specifically designed to remove pet hair from upholstery. The primary vacuum head has LED lights on the front and sides, and there’s also a crevice tool with an LED light for convenient cleaning in dark corners, along with a two-in-one dusting brush.

The vacuum has a touch-and-release button on the dustbin’s exterior to easily empty it without getting dust and pet dander on your hands.

Full Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Turbo Lift-Off Upright Vacuum Review

Our tester has six pets, so there’s plenty of mess to go around, whether it’s tracked-in dirt from muddy paws or scattered litter. Pulling out the upright vacuum for quick cleanups isn’t always convenient, and this cordless stick model is her go-to for daily maintenance.

One of the things she loves the most about the Levoit LVAC-300 is the five-stage filtration system, which provides air purifier-level purification, a must-have for pet owners with animals that shed or have lots of dander.

The vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—so she was able to adjust suction power depending on the size of the mess and debris. The LVAC-300 transitions between floor types easily, but excels on hardwood and tile.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself.

Full LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Tired of the pet hair tumbleweeds strewn about your floors? This robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. With 16,200 pascals of suction power, it effectively picked up debris from a variety of floor types such as carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile.

One of the most notable features is the built-in razor in the base station that automatically slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have to manually remove hair from the brush roll.

Beyond that, our tester felt that this robot vacuum successfully avoided pet toys, cords, and overly friendly animals that seemed very interested in the vacuum’s whereabouts.

There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper mop, and they extend outward to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards.

The companion app is helpful for managing cleaning schedules, monitoring battery levels, and mapping, but gets a little more confusing as you adjust more advanced smart features.

Full Eureka J15 Pro Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

We’re regularly testing vacuums with focused pet hair features, so it’s common to see different vacuums take the place of others in this roundup. Here are a few that we’ve tested and think are still worth recommending:

Dyson V16 Piston Animal: This is a newer release from the brand, with some of the highest suction power we’ve seen from a cordless stick vacuum. The all-floor head cleaner excelled on carpet, and hair never got tangled around the brush roll, but performance on hard surfaces wasn’t as impressive. The vacuum comes with the classic Fluffy Optic soft roller cleaner head, but for the “all-floor” cleaner head isn’t the most ideal for all surfaces.

Miele Guard L1 Cat and Dog Bagged Canister Vacuum: The cleaner head on this vacuum lifts to five heights, and the extra-long hose allows you to work your way around your home without lugging the entire base vacuum around with you. On the downside, it doesn’t clean high-pile carpeting like shag or tufted wool, and other models we recommend have better pet-hair-specific attachments for cleaning upholstery.

There are a few factors that make a vacuum well-suited for dog and cat fur—namely, how much hair its bin holds, how it empties, how well it filters fine particles, and the types of attachments included.

The ideal bin capacity depends on the size of your home’s dimensions and the amount of pet hair you usually manage on a regular basis. For households with multiple pets, or animals that shed heavily, a vacuum with a spacious bin capacity (one liter or more) reduces the number of times you have to empty it during cleaning.

If you have a smaller home or you just have one pet, a bin capacity of 0.5 to 1 liter will most likely suffice. If you’re still unsure of what you might need, here’s a breakdown of the bin capacity each type of vacuum typically offers.

These normally have the largest capacity, ranging from two to four liters to hold more pet hair, dander, and debris before needing to be emptied. This design and capability could be ideal for heavy-duty cleaning or households with more than one pet.

Upright vacuums come in a close second, often with a capacity between one and three liters, so they’re a good option for folks with a pet that sheds mildly, or only during part of the year. These vacuums are also sufficient for standard home cleaning.

Because cordless vacuums are better used as supplementary cleaning tools, they have much smaller dustbins—usually ranging between 0.3 and 0.7 liters—which is really only enough for spot-cleaning, picking up dust bunnies between deep cleaning sessions, and use in tight spaces.

Similar to cordless vacuums, robot vacuums live on the smaller end of bin capacity. If you decide to go with this type, I recommend a model with a self-emptying bin. Most robot vacuums have small onboard dustbins, but they fill up faster. Self-emptying models have a larger dust collection area in the base, so you won’t have to manually empty as frequently.

For allergy sufferers, it’s essential to have a vacuum with an excellent filtration system, so look for models with a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter. These filters trap 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. Pet dander can be as small as 2.5 microns in diameter, and a HEPA filter efficiently captures these particles along with pollen, dust, and other allergens your pets may have tracked into the house.

A fully sealed filtration system, sometimes called an anti-allergen seal, is another common feature on pet vacuums. This means the components of the vacuum are tightly sealed so fine particles can’t escape back into your home once they’ve been sucked up.

Powerful suction is vital, but the included tools and attachments are often what pet owners use to successfully pull hair out of upholstery and carpeting. The following attachments are useful for tackling pet hair, and they come with many of the models I recommend above.

A standard attachment that comes with almost all vacuums, these elongated, narrow tools are great for accessing tight areas, like behind the toilet or between couch cushions. They’re useful for cleaning up clumps of hair that may have gathered in corners of your home where the vacuum’s floor head cannot reach.

Non-motorized upholstery brushes have bristles or a strip of microfiber to clean off furniture. As you pull the tool across fabric, the bristles lift pet hair and dust to be sucked up through the vacuum hose.

For pet hair that’s worked deep into upholstery, whether on your furniture or in your car, a motorized pet tool provides the most lifting power. These tools have small, spinning brush rolls, usually equipped with bristles, that agitate hair to pull it from the fabric, and they tend to work much more efficiently than non-motorized tools.

If you have pet hair or dander on your window screens or baseboards, a dusting brush has long, soft bristles that pick up dust and fine particles without scratching surfaces.

In addition to an arsenal of attachments to pull up pet hair, there are a few features that make cleaning up after your dog or cat even easier.

#6307. A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Unlike in the Dr. Seuss tale, a swollen heart can be an alarming sign of stress or disease

The Grinch’s change of heart turned him from grumpy to radiating joy. Is such a transformation possible in real life?

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

“They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” says the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really big in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”

In one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

“Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson says. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand says, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson says.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too big to pump blood.

So instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.)

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as big as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”

#6306. In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia’s Puncak Jaya, and now what is left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields

Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.

In 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of New Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.

That’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.

It also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.

Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.

Next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.

Scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades.

NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.

Ice shows up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.

The area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.

An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana said.

The ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana said.

In 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.

Thinning ice also cracks apart. Each new piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.

In the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” said Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”

To count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.

On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana said.

El Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.

Fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.

During the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS. In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.

Then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.

Recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere.

BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040.

NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse.

The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment.

The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells.

"This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow, an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons.

The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals. Known as "SwAP-In," it enables researchers to rewrite large portions of an organism's genetic code by inserting big chunks of synthetic DNA. In this case, the approach was used to insert a human gene into lab mice.

"It is kind of a generic method that can be used to make extensively humanized mice," said study co-author Jef Boeke, director of the Institute for Systems Genetics at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a lead developer of the SwAP-In technique.

Liddelow anticipates that this new method for humanizing mice, or tweaking their biology to more closely match that of humans, will prove useful for studying a wide range of diseases, from common conditions like Alzheimer's to "orphan" diseases like XDP, which are rare, underresearched and lacking effective treatments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

XDP is a neurodegenerative condition that particularly impacts the striatum, part of the brain that's crucial for movement. The disease causes symptoms such as slowed movements, tremors, muscle stiffness and involuntary muscle contractions.

On average, symptoms emerge around age 39 and patients live for 13 to 16 years after their symptoms appear. In late stages of the disease, problems with breathing and swallowing can lead to deadly complications such as malnutrition, aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure. Historically, XDP has also carried a lot of social stigma, which has contributed to high rates of depression and suicide among those with the condition.

"Patients get sort of shunned and hidden away," Liddelow said. That, among other factors, made XDP difficult to study.

XDP shows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern (depicted above).

Although XDP isn't fully understood, its underlying genetic cause is known. It stems from a mutation in TAF1, a gene on the X chromosome that helps translate DNA sequences into new proteins. Because males carry only one X chromosome — and thus have no backup copy of the gene — the condition affects far more males than females.

The mutation first appeared in a person on Panay, an island in the Philippines. Due to a phenomenon called the "founder effect," it has risen in prevalence among people of Filipino ancestry but is not seen in other demographics, Boeke explained. Studies suggest there are about 5.7 cases per 100,000 people in the Philippines.

XDP's rarity and associated stigma have made the condition difficult to study, but there's another layer of complexity: The mutation in TAF1 was originally caused by a "jumping gene" ‪—‬ a bit of DNA that changed its position within the genome. In this instance, the DNA happened to jump into the middle of TAF1 and disrupted its function, Boeke said.

But the jumping gene in question is found only in primates. Ideally, if you wanted to study the disease in lab mice, you'd have to insert that jumping gene into their DNA — and that's exactly what the researchers did in the first of their two new studies.

Using SwAP-In, the team inserted 78,000 "letters" of human DNA code into mouse embryonic stem cells. This code included part of the human version of the TAF1 gene and the relevant jumping gene that causes XDP. In both lab dishes and living mice, this gene insertion triggered the telltale signs of XDP: low levels of the TAF1 protein, cell death and holes in the brain, especially in the striatum.

One big difference between mice and humans is that the mouse version of XDP progresses very quickly, with symptoms appearing in just 1.5 months, whereas the human disease takes years to show up. That may be because human bodies have safeguards to help offset the jumping gene's effects — at least for a while — while mice lack this safety net, the study authors theorized.

That difference in disease progression is actually a "huge advantage" for researchers, Boeke noted. "Because it's so sped up, it's possible to do experiments on therapeutics," he said. For instance, if an experimental drug is successfully fighting the disease, that should be obvious in the mice, whose condition would otherwise progress very quickly.

I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients.

In the second of the team's new studies, they took a closer look at the new mice with XDP, to see how the disorder affected their brain cells. Through a battery of tests, they realized that glial cells known as oligodendrocytes showed dramatic changes in both their overall numbers and their gene activity.

These cells would normally make a fatty insulating material called myelin, which wraps around the outgoing wires of neurons to help them send signals. To see how the cells were faring in the XDP mice, study co-author Priya Prakash, a postdoctoral scholar in Liddelow's lab, used a blue stain to label the cells within the mouse brain tissue.

"Where you would normally see this beautiful blue brain, full of lipid, full of myelin, you essentially see a white brain, with none of this lipid there," Liddelow said. This was especially apparent in the striatum and the prefrontal cortex.

Further experiments revealed that the mutation was preventing oligodendrocytes from fully maturing, and that reduced the amount of myelin made in these parts of the brain. They backed up these findings in brains of people with XDP that had been donated after death.

The researchers think this extensive loss of insulation may leave neurons vulnerable to dying early, Liddelow said. In short, "this is a neurodegenerative disease that may not first be manifesting in neurons themselves," he emphasized. "I think that is, one, interesting from a biological standpoint, but two, profoundly important for how you might develop therapies to help these patients."

Together, the studies raise several ideas for treating XDP. One treatment could involve cranking up the activity of the TAF1 gene to boost the levels of its related protein. This idea showed promise in experiments with mouse cells in the team's first paper. The second paper points to oligodendrocytes as potential targets for future therapies, and myelin loss as a potential early sign of the disease that might be useful for diagnosis.

There's still much more to learn about the biology of XDP and what types of treatments might reverse the drivers of the disease, Liddelow and Boeke emphasized. But now, other scientists have access to a brand-new mouse model that can help them solve the disease's remaining mysteries.

#6304. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV, D-W.Va., questions witnesses during a Senate Finance hearing on health care on June 23, 2011. (Scott J. Ferrell/CQ Roll Call)

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in New York City on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961. His passion was for the Far East and he spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as AmeriCorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, W.Va., in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness."

He had planned to remain only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family's long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected secretary of state.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “the hardest-working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with pneumoconiosis, or black lung disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in the Hart building, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor in June 2012. “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face reelection.

He had won reelection to the Senate handily during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was reelected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, and later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high health care costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

"These are people," Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. "Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice."

The amendment was rejected. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthening Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support the measure as it stood — he later added his support to the ACA, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation's mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller; four children: John D. Rockefeller V, Valerie Rockefeller, Charles Rockefeller and Justin Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-11.

#6303. The Book Lover’s Gift Guide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Science News staff loved books about dinosaurs, parenting and numbers in 2026

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science News staff devoured books of all kinds this year, on topics ranging from ecology and evolution to the human brain and mathematics. We covered it all — even a cookbook! These 10 titles rose to the top of our 2026 reading list and could make great gifts for the book lovers in your life. —  Anna Mattson, Assistant Editor

Big thinkers will love Huge Numbers, a fascinating look into the study of large numbers. “When I think of big numbers, I usually think of a 1 with a lot of zeroes tacked on the end. But the reality is much more complex than I ever imagined,” says senior physics writer Emily Conover. The book, among Conover’s favorites of the year, “provided me with a new appreciation of our number system and the creative ways mathematicians have expanded it to express ever-larger numbers,” she says. “Plus, contemplating unfathomably large figures makes my own concerns seem insignificant.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Staff writer Erin Garcia de Jesús’ favorite book of 2026, The Creatures’ Guide to Caring, will strike a chord with new parents. “Between sleepless nights and poopy diapers, there’s not much to laugh about in the early days of parenting. But I found plenty of humor (and plenty to be grossed out about) in The Creatures’ Guide to Caring,” Garcia de Jesús says. “It’s the perfect book to make anyone, parent or otherwise, feel better that we’re not the only animals struggling with our offspring.”

Merritt R. TuretskyW.W. Norton & Company | $29.99

Adventure seekers will lose themselves in the mesmerizing ecosystems at the heart of Bogland, biomedical sciences writer Aimee Cunningham’s favorite book of the year. Ecologist Merritt R. Turetsky immerses readers in these waterlogged landscapes that are often overlooked and underestimated. “I am firmly on team boglands after reading about the beauty and wonder of these ecosystems,” Cunningham says.

Senior writer Meghan Rosen’s favorite book of 2026 is perfect for anyone interested in — or wary of — health and wellness culture. Morbid exposes the lack of science behind a lot of antiaging advice, such as eating like centenarians do and taking “anti­aging” supplements. “Turns out, a lot of it is just plain bunk,” Rosen says. “Skeptical readers will enjoy Newman’s takedowns, which go down smoothly with a healthy dose of humor.”

Senior neuroscience writer Laura Sanders’ pick for 2026 is a must-read for any expecting mother, new mother or person looking to learn about how pregnancy and motherhood impact the body. “A Mother’s Brain reads like a scientific love letter to moms, who all too often get overlooked,” she says. Author and neuroscientist Susana Carmona “covers the nascent field of matrescence in lively, vivid chapters. And along the way, she convincingly argues that the maternal brain is compelling, wondrous and still mysterious,” Sanders says.

Those who listen to true crime podcasts or wish spooky season lasted all year long will enjoy Exhumed, an exploration of the lore and medical practices leading up to the 19th century New England vampire panic. “Thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down,” assistant editor Anna Mattson wrote in her online review. Mattson notes that Exhumed, her favorite read of 2026, is littered with bizarre facts that would be perfect for invigorating dull conversations.

For the anthropologist in your life, try The Story of Stories — a deep dive into how technological upheavals have shaped storytelling throughout history. The author provides what Sanders describes as scattershot history lessons in her online review: “Ashton has a knack for pulling out memorable bits from historical records, scientific studies and other sources for readers.”

Alexis Nikole NelsonSimon & Schuster | $35.00

Conover couldn’t pick just one favorite. For people who enjoy getting creative in the kitchen, she recommends Happy Snacking, Don’t Die! “This cookbook provides such a joyful how-to on foraging and eating wild plants,” Conover says. “It helped me see my plant neighbors in a whole new light. And I got to make some tasty treats to share with my family as well.”

Tyrant Lizard Queen is the only work of fiction on our list. But it’s rooted in real science, and stars a Tyrannosaurus rex. Author Riley Black “offers an empathetic look at a real-life creature that experienced hunger and pain, much like the animals that surround us today,” says Science News Explores assistant editor Aaron Tremper, who chose the book as his favorite of 2026. “Black’s penchant for story makes for a thrilling read that fans of Jurassic Park and King Kong can get behind.”

And for those interested in bioethics, we suggest picking up Every Living Creature. Author and physician Joshua D. Mezrich offers a comprehensive look at the field of xenotransplantation, through the stories of courageous doctors and patients who helped make it possible. “At times, the story can feel like a whirlwind, whisking readers across decades and from lab to lab and surgery to surgery,” Rosen wrote in her online review. “But at its core, Every Living Creature is a book about hope.”

#6301. Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet. They were short and came near eddies and fronts, hinting the fish check the ocean.

Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface. Every so often, one keeps going.

Satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). Nobody knows why the fish make them.

A team from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) has now looked at years of tagging data in search of an answer. The dives were short, fairly steady, and most common where surface temperatures varied and the sea surface stood higher. The authors think the fish may be sampling the water column, possibly to help them find their way. The study was published in Marine Biology.

Swordfish live in open oceans around the world, from about 45 degrees north to 45 degrees south. They follow a daily rhythm. By day they stay deep, usually between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet (400 and 700 meters), and at night they rise toward the surface.

That routine follows their food. Huge numbers of small animals live in the ocean’s twilight zone and move up and down each day, and swordfish track them. Like other large predators of the open sea, tuna and swordfish get much of their food from that dim layer.

Swordfish can handle water from about 36 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit (2 to 31 degrees Celsius). They keep their eyes and parts of their body warmer than the surrounding water, which helps them stay deep for long periods.

The researchers combined data from 34 pop-up satellite tags placed on North Atlantic swordfish between 2003 and 2024. Twenty-three were tagged off the Atlantic coast of Florida, six near the Grand Banks off Canada, three in the southern Sargasso Sea and two in the Gulf of America, also known as the Gulf of Mexico. Twenty-four were probably adults and 10 were probably juveniles.

The tags stayed on for one to six months and logged depth, temperature and light. Together, they covered 3,666 days of swordfish life.

The data came from a partnership with NOAA’s Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

“It wouldn’t have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab,” said Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and an author of the study.

The team flagged 39 days on which a fish went unusually deep for its own normal pattern. On 25 of those days, recorded by 10 tags, the data were detailed enough to confirm a distinct extreme dive.

These dives averaged about 3,250 feet (991 meters) at their deepest point, and the deepest reached roughly 5,460 feet (1,664 meters), more than a mile down. On ordinary days, the fish’s deepest point averaged about 2,090 feet (637 meters).

A single extreme dive lasted about 45 to 55 minutes on average. When a fish made one such dive in a day, it usually dropped two to three times faster than it climbed back. In one fish’s full-resolution record, it spent between a few seconds and about six minutes at the bottom.

The water at the bottom of these dives averaged about 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8.4 degrees Celsius). On other days, the coldest water the fish met averaged about 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12.1 degrees Celsius).

Most dives started and ended in the twilight zone, during daylight. In 12 of 16 such dives, the fish came back to within about 33 feet (10 meters) of the depth where it began.

The authors weighed seven possible reasons for deep dives, including feeding, escaping predators, saving energy and navigation.

Feeding seemed unlikely. A hunting fish would be expected to linger at depth, but these fish barely paused at the bottom before heading back up. The dives also did not cluster at dawn and dusk, when prey is easiest to reach.

Escape did not fit well either. The descents were steady, about 3.3 feet (1 meter) per second, and the fish behaved normally afterward. Only one dive began and ended near the surface at night, when the authors think predators may be more likely to be around. The authors could not rule out that the two juveniles, which made several dives in a single day, were avoiding predators.

Extreme dives were much more likely where sea surface temperature varied a lot and where the sea surface stood higher. In the team’s model, each extra degree Celsius of temperature variation made a dive about 23 times more likely. These conditions mark swirling eddies, fronts and major currents such as the Gulf Stream.

The authors suggest that crossing into a new water mass may prompt a swordfish to check what lies below. Short, repeatable dives of the same shape would fit that kind of sampling.

“They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses,” said Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program and now works at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Deeper water could also give a clearer reading of Earth’s magnetic field, which many fish can sense, away from the busy, changing layers near the surface. Some dives happened near seamounts, ridges and magnetic anomalies, but those links were weak, though rough seafloor showed a smaller but significant effect. Other ocean travelers are under similar suspicion, as oceanic manta rays also dive deep, apparently not to feed.

The authors stress that their conclusions are inferences. Satellite tag positions carry an average error of about 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 kilometers), and possibly more for deep divers like swordfish. That makes it hard to match a dive to a specific seafloor feature.

It is still unclear how common these dives are among swordfish, and whether they differ between populations or ages.

Swordfish support valuable fisheries, so knowing what steers them could help predict where they go as the ocean changes.

The information was obtained from the study published in Marine Biology and from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6300. Trump names Stephen Miller his chief of staff ahead of Dem takeover

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, talks with reporters at the White House on April 28. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, the architect of the hard-line immigration and deportation program voters rejected this week, will become White House chief of staff.

Susie Wiles will depart that post and move to the Trump political organization, which appears to be in full operation, even after the president's last midterm election. Miller has been deputy chief of staff, overseeing the Trump administration's domestic policy.

Miller’s first day will be Monday, Trump said in a social media post.

Trump dubbed Miller “one of my most trusted advisors” and said Wiles, who also oversaw his 2024 presidential campaign, “has done an outstanding job.”

Wiles, who Trump recently announced had won a battle with breast cancer, said in a X post that “serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” adding she was “proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

The chief-of-staff change came three days after Republicans were demolished in Trump’s final midterm election, with House Democrats on pace for the largest majority in over a decade and at least a 54-seat Senate majority come January.

Trump addressed the personnel move as he departed the White House Friday for an event and weekend in Florida — though he ignored a question about his recent declaration that Wiles would be sticking around.

“I wanted to make a change,” he said in a roughly three-minute exchange with reporters before he walked to Marine One. “Sometimes in life, you have to make moves.”

Trump in recent days had become open to working with Democrats after the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, even after railing against what he called the party’s “bad” policy during an October-long campaign rally blitz.

“Look, I mean, I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive,” Trump told reporters Wednesday. “But I have the power of the veto. So if we don't like what they're doing… They've already called and they want to talk about things. And that's fine.”

Trump summoned Thursday's press pool into the Oval Office for an executive order signing. On his desk was a red baseball cap with "VETO" across the front in large white lettering.

Miller has worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to several GOP lawmakers, including former Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., who became attorney general in Trump's first administration.

But making the hard-line Miller his White House chief of staff even before congressional Democrats get organized likely will draw the ire of the incoming majority.

Virginia Rep. Donald S. Beyer Jr. was among the first Democratic lawmakers to slam Trump’s decision.

“Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller doubles down on the politics of hatred, lawlessness, and failure that the American people soundly rejected three days ago,” Beyer said in a statement. "Miller embodies the worst elements of the Trump presidency. His promotion shows that Trump has learned nothing from his electoral debacle and has no intention of even trying to work constructively with the next Congress.”

Many congressional Democrats — leaders, returning incumbents and members-elect — want to investigate Trump, his inner circle and family members while also pursuing a legislative agenda aimed at paring the cost of living.

To that end, as chief of staff, Democrat-run committees calling Miller to testify is highly unlikely since he could continue to claim executive privilege. That allows senior White House aides to withhold many internal West Wing communications, documents, and presidential-related conversations and actions, from lawmakers.

In public comments and television interviews, Miller has accused Democrats of being aligned with figures and candidates who “hate” Americans, and once said the party is “unworthy of power.”

“So the Democrats have become a party of freaks, weirdos, losers and crazies,” Miller said during a July appearance on Fox News. “But you can’t laugh it off because it’s deadly serious. When you give these people power, everything you know and love in this world falls apart. You have chaos, corruption, decay, violence, poverty.”
