#6243. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

#6241. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6240. This 9-Year-Old Owns Dozens of Vintage Toilets. He May Have Found His Calling in Plumbing—and Is Inspiring Others.

The U.S. is facing a trades crisis. Fostering some unique hobbies may be the fix we desperately need.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

Like most kids his age, 9-year-old Damian Skaer loves YouTube. Unlike most kids his age, Damian also loves toilets, a passion he discovered on the social media platform.

Now, he’s a social media star himself, showing off his growing collection of vintage toilets to hundreds of thousands of followers across TikTok and Instagram: a pale yellow 1965 American Standard Cadet, a robin’s egg-blue 1963 Crane Oxford, and a 1972 Kohler Wellworth the color of an army tank. Standing on the 11-toilet, fully plumbed platform his dad built in the family’s Eastern Washington backyard, Damian points out their trapways, the fill valves, the siphon jets, the lid bolts, and, of course, the pièce de resistance—the flush.

Roger Skaer, Damian’s dad, says his son’s obsession began a few years ago. “He stumbled across these plumbers on YouTube who replace toilets, test them, fix them, and, man, he just loves watching videos of people working on toilets,” Roger says. “There’s been a lot of engineering behind toilet evolution over the last 100 years, and he’s fascinated by it.”

Damian’s collection began when he found a couple of old toilets in his grandparents’ barn. Since then, he has amassed about 40, according to Roger. Each week, new models arrive from brands looking to collaborate with the 9-year-old.

While the topic of young people and screens continues to cause serious consternation among adults, for some kids, they’re serving as an introduction to the skilled trades, occupations like carpentry, welding, and plumbing that have struggled to attract and retain new talent. According to a 2026 National Association of House Builders survey, only 6 percent of young adults 18 to 25 planned to pursue a career in construction trades.

But a crop of young social media influencers are bucking that trend. Guiseppe D’Anna has been working on cars at his dad’s collision repair shop since he was six; today Guiseppe’s Garage has a quarter-million followers on YouTube, and the automotive wunderkind is on “a mission to help shape the next generation of gearheads.” British woodworker Gabriel River Clark has been creating DIY content since he was 12, crafting anything from dinnerware to toys to home decor. On TikTok, 10-year-old Jackson Laux, a.k.a. Just a Jackson Thing, delights his roughly million followers with his deep knowledge of vintage tractors and mowers.

This kind of early exposure is vital to promoting trade occupations, says Paul Goodrum, PhD, a professor in Construction Engineering and Management at the University of Colorado Boulder. While lots of kids used to learn these skills in high school shop or career tech classes, over the past few decades, policy makers and administrators have phased vocational educational courses out of high school curriculums, emphasizing core academic subjects and college readiness instead. The best vocational programs, according to Goodrum, tend to exist in alternative schools for students with behavioral challenges.

“There is a bit of a disconnect between how we measure the quality of our schools and what the economy and the workforce needs in this country,” he says. “As an industry, we really need to be trying to more actively expose kids to these career paths not just in high school but middle school too.”

But it’s a vicious cycle, Goodrum says: fewer trades workers mean fewer teachers to teach vocational classes, “and how do you convince someone to give up a really high-paying job to go teach high school?”

The shortage of skilled workers is creating headaches for more than just hiring managers. A reduced workforce is causing construction project costs to soar and go over schedule. It’s also turning worksites into danger zones, as understaffed crews are working longer hours at a brutal pace. In 2024, construction workers accounted for about one in five workplace deaths in the country.

Most workers who end up in trade occupations do so later in life, often as a second career. The average age of an apprentice in a construction program is 28, for instance, while plumbing and electrical apprentices are often pushing 40.

“For so long we nurtured this culture saying you’ve got to go to college and get this degree or that degree, and if you end up working in construction it was because you somehow failed,” says Roger Skaer, a trained carpenter. “I think it’s a product of a long-lived, misguided representation of what success should look like.”

Recently, young people have started to question that college-or-bust narrative. Between 2020 and 2025, enrollment in two-year vocational or trade schools grew by almost 20 percent. And while the trades have their own difficulties—dangerous work conditions, wear and tear on the body—they offer something lots of other fields can’t right now: job security. According to the New Hampshire–based nonprofit Bring Back the Trades, more than 1.4 million trade jobs will be vacant in 2030.

Roger is confident that eventually Damian will fill one of those positions. “Right now, he’s saying plumber, I’m thinking maybe a toilet designer,” he says, explaining that Damian’s been angling for a 3D printer so that he can build his own commodes. “I truly feel he's going to be in some kind of trade or hands-on craftwork.”

And if toilets don’t pan out, Damian has a backup hobby: washer and dryer installation and repair.

#6239. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

California Rep. Ken Calvert walks down the House steps after votes on Sept. 3. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6238. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6236. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6235. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, here at a hearing in July, has won a sixth term representing the 9th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

#6234. 18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

I've traveled to some pretty far-flung places, but nothing could have prepared me for the logistical circus of vacationing with a baby. Four years and 30 countries later, my son Julian has taught me a thing or two about what makes a resort genuinely welcoming to its littlest guests. For starters, there’s a massive difference between a hotel that hands your kid a coloring book at check-in and one that has anticipated the thousands of little things that can make or break a family vacation.

The best resorts for infants and toddlers also understand that keeping littles happy isn’t a one-size-fits-all proposition. A baby might need a quiet nursery and a reliable nanny; a three-year-old might be thrilled to feed goats on an Austrian farm, explore a Japanese forest, or make plaster casts of lion tracks in the Kalahari. And parents? Sometimes we just want to eat dinner without having to negotiate with a tiny inquisitor.

That kind of thoughtfulness is what sets the properties on this list apart. I’ve seen it firsthand at more than half a dozen of them, where the greatest luxury wasn’t necessarily the thread count or the size of the swimming pool, but getting to enjoy a five-star vacation instead of merely financing one for your offspring. Read on for the best resorts for infants and toddlers.

Location: Savusavu, FijiPrice: From $1,136 per night

Jet lag aside, this is one of the rare luxury resorts where traveling with a child feels not just doable, but deeply supported. Every family with a child under five is assigned two dedicated nannies—one for daytime adventures, one for evenings—so parents can book a snorkeling trip with the resident marine biologist or linger over a blissfully kid-free dinner. When my son and I arrived in 2024—the first international stop on our 88-day, 14-country trip—it took me all of four minutes to abandon any guilt I had about dropping him off. His nanny was warm, attentive, and completely unfazed by toddlers being toddlers; she whisked him away for glass-bottom boat rides, hermit crab hunts, and splashes in the resort’s “mushroom-cascade” wading pool.

Parents of even younger children will appreciate the made-to-order purées and unlimited milk supply; nurseries stocked with infant cots, toys, and baby baths; and daily laundry service and disposable diapers for sale in the on-site boutique. Following a spring 2026 renovation, the resort now has five two-bedroom bures (a traditional Fijian hut or cabin), giving families more room to spread out. The Bula Club—essentially a resort within a resort—has a sun-safe junior pool with a waterslide, trampoline, and tricycles.

Location: Flamands Beach, St. BartsPrice: From $805 per night

With 61 rooms, suites, and villas, Cheval Blanc is one of the glammest maisons on an island full of glammy maisons. The inn has even partnered with high-end Parisian baby accessories brand Baudou to spoil its style-conscious guests. Cots are dressed in the finest linens, and rooms include a changing table with a diaper basket and baby care products, a rattan high chair with a cushioned seat, baby-friendly crockery, and a hand-stitched bib embroidered with seahorses and stars. Wee beach towels and a selection of beach toys are available for afternoon romps on Flamands, one of the prettiest powder-white beaches in St. Barts. At the new Le Carrousel play space, children ages 3 to 12 can climb aboard an imaginary exploration vessel, tumble into a coconut-themed ball pit, and discover the island’s Arawak history through interactive storytelling. Come mealtime, they can indulge in made-to-order baby purées prepared by the in-house culinary team. Upon request, a professional photographer can be brought to the premises to document your family trip.

Location: West End, AnguillaPrice: From $725 per night

Toddlers are greeted with custom Anguilla-themed stuffies, pint-sized bathrobes, and slippers at this upscale resort on Anguilla’s West End, where accommodations range from contemporary-chic guest rooms to five-bedroom beachfront villas, some with private pools and kitchens. Wherever you rest your head, expect kids to squeal when they catch a glimpse of the iguanas that freely roam the property. The zero-entry Bamboo Pool has mini loungers for infants; other five-star amenities include complimentary cribs, strollers, car seats, bottle sterilizers, baby tubs, Le Petit Prince toiletries, SlumberPods, and organic puréed baby food on the room service menu. A refreshed splash pad offers another place for little ones to cool off, while children five and under eat free from the kids menu throughout the resort. Also notable: American Airlines operates year-round nonstop flights from Miami, while AnguillAir offers seasonal service from Boston, Newark, and Baltimore, so families no longer have to hitch a ride over from St. Maarten.

Location: Karatu, TanzaniaPrice: From $518 per adult per night, including full board

After a long-haul flight with a toddler, Gibb’s Farm feels like an exhale. Set on 80 acres of organic gardens and coffee groves on the forested outer slopes of the Ngorongoro Crater, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, the property is an ideal place to begin or end a safari. My son was only 20 months old when we stayed here, but we happily spent hours roaming the gardens, chasing chickens, and learning how to milk cows. The farm’s one-bedroom cottages—many decorated with pieces from Gibb’s unique artist-in-residence program—are ideal for families, offering private terraces, outdoor showers, and enough breathing room for mid-tantrum resets.

There’s no kids club, but toddlers are warmly embraced here. The staff arranged a private game drive for us so we could move at Julian’s pace, stopping for snack breaks and diaper changes as needed. In the crater—home to one of the densest populations of large mammals in Africa—we saw lions, hippos, warthogs, wildebeest, and flamingos, but it was the dazzle of zebras milling around our vehicle that most delighted my son. Back on the farm, little ones can collect eggs, feed the pigs, wander among the coffee shrubs, splash in the pool, or learn about the music and customs of the local Iraqw tribe through hands-on cultural activities.

Location: Palm Beach, FloridaPrice: From $890 per night

Florida is a perennially popular destination for young families, and no resort rolls out the red carpet for babies better than the Breakers Palm Beach. Founded in 1896, the luxury hotel has a private beach and four oceanfront pools, including a zero-entry one designed specifically for youngsters. There’s also a 4,500-square-foot playground with slides, tunnels, and bridges, plus the new Seaside Family Entertainment Center, a beachfront hub with a dedicated Toddler Cove, arts and crafts, and interactive games. Cribs, infant baths, bottle warmers, and strollers are available upon request, as is the childproofing of guest rooms, which involves padding perilously edged furniture, covering electrical sockets, and removing trash bags from cans. Bicycles with baby seats and children’s bikes are available to rent, as are private poolside bungalows with a dedicated concierge standing by, ready to fetch popsicles and pool toys at a moment’s notice. Other big wins for tiny visitors: poolside spin art, Build-A-Bear workshops, and daily children’s programming.

Location: Punta Cana, Dominican RepublicPrice: From $850 per night

For parents seeking a more home-like environment, the multi-bedroom villas at this secluded Relais & Chateaux property offer spacious living rooms, full kitchens, and private pools. Staff arrange scavenger hunts and arts and crafts hours; for an additional $325, parents can reserve the VIBabies package. This comes with two hours of complimentary babysitting plus a host of handy gear—including a portable crib (with turndown service!), a changing table, diapers, a bottle warmer, a baby monitor, an infant tub, pool alarms, a Baby Einstein play table, a 4moms MamaRoo baby swing, and a basket of kid-approved snacks and juices. For fun in the sun, Eden Roc will throw in a pop-up beach playpen, swim nappies, and sun protection gear (a bucket hat, colored sunglasses, Nivea sun lotion, and aloe vera gel) for use at the sandy beach and artificial lagoon.

Location: Nuevo Nayarit, MexicoPrice: From $454 per adult per night

Families vacationing at this AAA Five Diamond resort on the Riviera Nayarit are assigned a baby concierge who coordinates all meals and nanny services. Whatever gear you don’t want to drag from home—crib, stroller, baby tub and toiletries, bottle brush and sterilizer, pacifier, floaties—the team can arrange for on-site, all complimentary. Parents checking in with infants also receive a sleep guide developed with pediatric sleep consultant Rachael Shepard-Ohta of Hey Sleepy Baby, with tips for managing time zone changes and maintaining bedtime routines on the road. The kids club is stocked with books, blocks, and a play kitchen; parents may additionally request a crib mobile, rattle, or teether for use in the room.

Some suites have private plunge pools, but the hotel jewel is the triple-tiered, multi-temperature infinity pool. Mini cabanas await down at the beach, along with hooded baby towels and fresh-squeezed juice. Young spa-goers can opt for a gentle sunrise massage soundtracked by Mozart or a chocolate explosion face mask, then strike a pose with mom or dad during a baby yoga class. Executive chef Guillaume Morancé and his team prepare gourmet purées to challenge young palates (think white fish with celery, leeks, and mushroom) at every meal. The resort even offers a Mi Primer Fiesta package for celebrating a baby's first birthday, complete with piñatas and foam.

Location: Koh Yao Yai, ThailandPrice: From $308 per night

Set on one of the Andaman’s last unspoiled islands—reachable only by boat and blissfully free of traffic—this resort feels worlds away from the party throngs on Phuket and Krabi. When Julian and I visited in 2024, it was during a vintage sidecar tour through rubber plantations and rice fields that I realized how special this island really is: no honking, no rush, just villagers waving as you pass. The accommodations were a slam dunk too: Family suites with bunk beds and tipi play tents come stocked with baby tubs, bottle warmers, sterilizers, baby chairs, and toys. The Grand Family Suite ups the ante with a chocolate treasure box at check-in, while all families with children receive a treasure map. Ground-floor suites open directly onto the resort’s enormous family pool, while infants and early swimmers have dedicated splash zones and shallow areas. As a bonus, the staff truly adores kids—one affable pool attendant peeled off his socks and shoes and joined my son on the slides when he saw how happy it made him.

Pristine beach and pools aside, the resort is home to southern Thailand’s largest kids club, featuring climbing walls, a dance stage, and an epic ball pit. Parents can join kids under six for Junior Explorer activities like kite making, batik painting, and sandcastle building, or arrange a family excursion to go island-hopping by longtail boat. For something even more tailored, little ones can try Muay Thai lessons, aerial yoga, or beach fishing with locals.

Location: Beaver Creek, ColoradoPrice: From $275 per night

Ask anyone who has ever attempted skiing with a toddler—it takes an act of Congress just to get them into a snowsuit. What saved my sanity at Park Hyatt Beaver Creek was that the slopes were, quite literally, outside our front door. This 189-room, chateau-style property is one of only two true ski-in, ski-out hotels at the base of Beaver Creek Mountain Resort, and that convenience is priceless. I could bundle up my kiddo and hand him off to a private instructor at the Ski and Snowboard School (open to ages three and up) and know that he was in eternally patient hands. After his post-lesson hot chocolates, Julian burned off whatever energy he had left in the family game room and the snowy outdoor playground before splashing around in the heated pool and hot tubs—his preferred après.

Location: Palm Desert, CaliforniaPrice: From $348 per night, including a $45 daily resort fee

This 450-acre resort features a 12,000-square-foot arcade—the largest hotel arcade in California. This is great news for kids of all ages who are stoked to play retro video games, test their skills in high-tech simulators, or try their hand at duckpin bowling. Family by JW programming gets the whole gang together with seasonal arts and crafts, fish feedings, movie nights, and more. Tots will also love meeting the property’s flock of Chilean flamingos, practicing their putt-putt on the 18-hole miniature golf course, and ordering off the children’s menus available at all on-site dining outlets. Families can also hop aboard boats departing from the hotel lobby for a cruise along the resort’s waterways.

Location: Chicago, IllinoisPrice: From $129 per night

The Loews Loves Families initiative, available at 27 properties throughout North America, is one of the most baby-friendly hotel offerings around. Guest rooms are equipped with mini fridges and kettles for storing and sanitizing bottles; full-size cribs, baby tubs, and night-lights are complimentary. Housekeeping will cover electrical outlets and supply foam bumpers upon request, and kids are given a cute amenity kit with baby lotion, wipes, shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. Board games, coloring books, pool toys, and iPads preloaded with movies and games are available from the concierge desk, as is a family activity guide highlighting the best local options for museums, zoos, and kid-friendly restaurants. There’s even a Bedtime Book Cart to help parents maintain their routine while on the road.

Location: Sagres, PortugalPrice: From $149 per night

At Martinhal Sagres, a stylish beachfront resort tucked inside a protected natural park in Portugal’s Algarve, the littlest guests get the VIP treatment. A baby concierge stocks rooms with cribs, bottle sterilizers, high chairs, and other essentials before families arrive—sparing parents the frustration of hauling half the nursery overseas. Even better, the resort’s supervised kids clubs welcome infants as young as six months, with separate programs for crawling babies, curious toddlers, and older children. Accommodations range from contemporary hotel suites to spacious villas with kitchens and washing machines; other perks include five swimming pools, sandy playgrounds, and restaurants offering dedicated baby menus. The Baby's First Holiday package sweetens the deal with a couples massage and romantic dinner—babysitting included.

Location: Oklahoma City, OklahomaPrice: From $149 per night, inclusive of water park access for two people

Operated by the Chickasaw Nation, this 404-room property blends big-ticket family fun with a strong sense of place. When Julian and I visited, it was the cultural aspect that surprised us most—especially the Chickasaw-curated gallery and easy access to the Smithsonian-affiliated First Americans Museum next door, which recently debuted the fully immersive FAMily Discovery Center. Outside, the 4.5-acre lagoon complex boasts the fourth-largest pool in the country—complete with zip-line plunges, an inflatable obstacle course, and an adults-only swim-up bar for parents who need a moment of respite. Inside, the 100,000-square-foot water park is kept at a blissful 82 degrees and features a low tide pool with pint-sized splash structures that didn’t overwhelm my budding swimmer.

There’s an arcade, mirror maze, and candy store, plus a slew of specialty eateries serving the four main food groups for toddlers: hot dogs, pizza, ice cream, and tacos. On Friday and Saturday evenings, there’s even a storytelling Pajama Hour led by resort staff at the lobby fireplace, with bedtime attire encouraged. Families will appreciate the value here: Children under two stay free, and spacious suites offer bunk beds and semi-private sleeping areas, with cribs available on request.

Location: Puerto Morelos, MexicoPrice: From $420 per night

As far as resorts for families go, Sensira, an all-inclusive luxury resort on the Riviera Maya, sure knows how to make a kid feel special. The Baby Explorer Club, designed for ages 18 months through 3 years, has indoor slides, bounce houses, and a ball pit, plus supervised sensory activities, music, and storytelling. For families with older kids in tow, there’s a movie theater, miniature golf course, zip line, water park, basketball court, tennis court, climbing wall, gaming stations, indoor trampoline park, and two swimming pools (there's a third pool designated for adults only).

The hotel can prepare fresh purées on request for infants and toddlers and has a kids corner at the buffet with food displayed at little ones’ eye level. It also supplies all the equipment parents need for a hassle-free stay, including bottle warmers and sterilizers, full-size cribs, and car seats. Babysitting services are available from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily, and parents are given a beeper to stay in touch. (If an infant is still breastfeeding, the nanny will fetch a parent for mealtime.) Even the spa takes family well-being into consideration, offering a full slate of all-ages wellness programming, including gentle therapies for children and teens that mirror adult rituals, and purpose-built family treatment cabins.

Location: Crete, GreecePrice: From $199 per night

Phāea Cretan Malia is one of those rare design hotels that’s as thoughtfully geared toward families with babies and toddlers as it is toward style-hungry adults. The low-rise, modernist buildings sit in lush, shady gardens that keep the grounds cool even in peak summer heat. When Julian and I stayed here in 2024, we spent hours pinballing from the sandy, shallow beach to the swimming pools to the Tiny Explorers’ Club—a padded, sunlit playroom for ages three and under where parents can spend time with their little ones.

For ages 3–12, the Little Explorers Kids Club has its own kitchen for baking sessions, a mini stage for dance and theater, an environmental play area, an organic garden to tend, and an outdoor playground—a godsend when little ones have energy to burn. Parents can also request the Baby Package, available for an additional charge, which includes babysitting services and toddler gear to cut down on packing. And while the open-air restaurants serve gorgeous Cretan dishes built around local produce, they’re equally prepared for picky palates: think wood-fired pizzas, simple pastas, and fresh fruit. When you’re ready to venture out, Potamos Beach and the Minoan ruins of Malia Palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, are an easy walk away.

Location: Southern Kalahari, South AfricaPrice: From around $7,000 per night for two adults, all-inclusive

Taking a toddler on safari sounds like a terrible idea until you discover Tswalu, South Africa’s largest privately protected conservation area, in the malaria-free Kalahari. At Loapi, six stand-alone safari homes with one or two bedrooms have private plunge pools, chefs, house managers, and dedicated guides, trackers, and vehicles—meaning no one cares if your child talks incessantly through a lion sighting. (Mine certainly did.)

When we visited in August 2026, Julian raced our guide and tracker through the red dunes, dictated his pasta preferences to the chef, and played catch with his child minder while I squeezed in some work. The flexibility is extraordinary: Game drives can be tailored around naps and short attention spans while older siblings can learn archery and animal tracking through the Junior Ranger program. Other highlights include close-up encounters with habituated meerkats and some of the best stargazing I've experienced anywhere. We also spotted black-maned lions, cheetahs, wild dogs, and desert black rhinos, but some of Julian’s happiest moments were spent chasing a ball with the staff. For families seeking a (slightly) less extravagant safari, Tswalu’s Motse camp offers one- and two-bedroom suites and shared facilities; its five-bedroom Tarkuni homestead is another option for multigenerational groups of up to 10.

Location: Atami, Shizuoka Prefecture, JapanPrice: From $238 per night

Less than an hour by bullet train from Tokyo, Risonare Atami sits high above a Japanese seaside town famous for its hot springs and fireworks festivals. All 81 rooms overlook Sagami Bay, with some offering front-row views of the town’s fireworks displays. The resort’s Baby-Friendly Stay Plan outfits spacious rooms with cribs and other infant necessities, while the restaurants serve complimentary rice porridge and vegetable purées. Parents can even hand off children as young as six months to an in-house nursery for up to 150 minutes of complimentary childcare while they tuck into a multicourse kaiseki dinner at the hotel’s restaurant, Hanabi.

Little ones have a heated indoor pool with a shallow splash zone and an ocean-view playroom with a ball pit and toddler-friendly climbing wall. Outdoors, Kusu Kusu centers on a tree house built into a 300-year-old camphor tree, with forest treasure hunts for children ages two and up and a treetop obstacle course for older kids. Parents can also steal away to the resort's semi-open-air onsen overlooking the bay.

Location: Grossarl, AustriaPrice: From $669 per night, including full board and childcare

Part luxury Alpine retreat, part working organic farm, Moar Gut is a five-star family resort where children can feed goats, cuddle rabbits, and even “adopt” an animal to care for during their stay. Set on a sprawling car-free estate in Austria’s Grossarl Valley, the 46-suite property takes its back-to-nature philosophy seriously. Its 10,000-square-foot kids club is built from natural materials like wood, linen, and sheep’s wool, with a painting studio, woodworking workshops, and guided forest adventures. Even babies get the full Alpine treatment: The separate nursery, offering supervised care from 30 days old, has Swiss stone pine cribs, organic bedding, and hay-covered walls. At the Lillee Baby Spa, parents can book guided infant massage, yoga, or floating sessions starting at three weeks old. Older children can ride ponies, forage for alpine herbs, and bake traditional Austrian treats, while parents have an adults-only spa and six-course farm-to-table dinners to look forward to. There's even a dedicated organic baby buffet with fresh purées and formula.

What is the best destination to travel to with an infant and/or toddler?

For a first trip with a baby or toddler, destinations with manageable flight times, reliable medical care, and resorts that minimize the logistical headaches of traveling with little ones are ideal. Florida, Mexico, and the Caribbean are excellent starting points, with direct flights from many US cities, and resorts that cater specifically to young children. Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla is one standout, offering complimentary baby equipment, a zero-entry family pool, and a splash pad. For families ready to venture farther, Portugal's Algarve is another excellent choice, especially Martinhal Sagres, where supervised childcare starts at six months. In the Austrian Alps, Moar Gut goes a step further, welcoming infants as young as 30 days into its professionally staffed nursery.

Are there any good all-inclusive resorts for infants and toddlers?

Absolutely. Jean-Michel Cousteau Resort in Fiji is particularly impressive, with meals, activities, and dedicated nanny care included in the rate. Children under six are assigned two nannies who work opposite shifts, providing personalized care throughout the day and evening, while older children are paired with Fijian companions who guide them through age-appropriate activities. Closer to home, Grand Velas Riviera Nayarit in Mexico features gourmet dining, a baby concierge who arranges infant equipment and coordinates meals and childcare, and specialty purées for its youngest guests (babysitting costs extra).

What resort in the US is best for families with infants and toddlers?

The Breakers Palm Beach in Florida is hard to beat. Its private beach and zero-entry family pool are ideal for little swimmers, while a 4,500-square-foot playground and the Seaside Family Entertainment Center—with its dedicated Toddler Cove—give youngsters room to burn off energy. The hotel can also supply cribs, strollers, and bottle warmers, as well as childproof guest rooms upon request. Parents, meanwhile, get the restaurants, spa, and old-school Palm Beach glamour that have made The Breakers a fixture on luxury travel lists for generations.

#6233. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”
