#6141. Here’s Why The Boeing 777X Won’t Let Pilots Take Off With Its Wings Still Folded

The Boeing 777X cannot take off with its wingtips folded due to critical safety and aerodynamic reasons. The extended wingtips are essential for the 777X's designed lift and fuel efficiency. Taking off with them folded would significantly increase drag and reduce lift, potentially compromising the aircraft's safety during the critical takeoff phase.

While the 777X is physically capable of remaining airborne with its wingtips folded, it is strictly prohibited and operationally restricted from doing so by both design and regulation. The aircraft is equipped with escalating warning systems that alert pilots if the wingtips are not extended and locked before entering a runway. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) certification requires these systems to effectively prevent the aircraft from taking off in a folded configuration.

The 777X uses a revolutionary wingtip folding system designed and manufactured by Liebherr-Aerospace at its center of excellence in Lindenberg, Germany. This system is a first for commercial aviation and allows the aircraft to maintain high-efficiency aerodynamics in flight while fitting into standard airport gates designed for smaller aircraft.

The 3.5-meter (approx. 11 feet) wingtips are operated by a complex actuation system that transitions them between folded (vertical) and extended (horizontal) positions. The movement is driven by a hydraulic power drive unit (PDU) and geared rotary actuators. The full transition takes approximately 20 seconds.

Once extended, the wingtips are secured by latch-pin and secondary-lock actuators. During flight, the mechanism is mechanically locked with a large bolt and electronically isolated. This ensures the wingtips cannot move even if there is a power failure.

A wider wingspan moves the wingtip vortices further away from the fuselage. This reduces the downwash on the wing, allowing it to generate more lift with less drag. The larger surface area creates more lift, reducing the thrust required from the GE9X engines to stay airborne. This results in a roughly 10%-12% improvement in fuel efficiency compared to previous generations and competitors.

The 777X integrates advanced aerodynamics with digital flight controls to deliver a ride that is significantly more efficient and comfortable than its predecessors. The extra span enables the 777X to climb faster and cruise at higher, more efficient altitudes where air resistance is lower.

Made from carbon-fiber reinforced plastic, these wings are thinner and lighter than traditional aluminum wings. This allows for the massive span without a prohibitive weight penalty. With GE9X engines, these aerodynamics result in lower fuel burn than competing aircraft like the Airbus A350, and a 20% lower fuel consumption rate than the legacy 747, which it is designed to replace.

The 777X features Smooth Ride Technology, an advanced fly-by-wire system adapted from the 787 Dreamliner, designed to neutralize turbulence actively. Hundreds of sensors detect air disturbances in real-time. The flight computer then automatically actuates the control surfaces, specifically the flaperons, to damp vertical motion and pitch that passengers feel during turbulence.

The highly flexible composite wings act like giant shock absorbers, bending and flexing during flight to absorb gust loads rather than transmitting those forces directly to the cabin. Beyond the ride quality,the 777X offers a lower cabin altitude (6,000 feet) and higher humidity. These environmental improvements, combined with 40% less engine noise, help reduce jet lag and physical fatigue on long-haul flights.

The folding mechanism is not designed to handle the massive aerodynamic loads encountered during takeoff and flight while in the "up" position. Attempting a flight with them folded could lead to mechanical failure or the tips breaking off.

Boeing integrated multiple fail-safes into the flight systems to prevent such an occurrence. If the wingtips are not extended and locked, the aircraft's takeoff warning system (required by the FAA and EASA) will trigger a loud alarm when the pilot adds power.

Boeing implemented an electronic checklist that confirms the position of the wingtips. If the flight crew attempts to initiate a takeoff procedure, the system will indicate “incomplete” until the wingtips are extended. If the pilots begin to take off roll without extending the wingtips, the avionics in the 777x will no longer trigger an aborted takeoff once the plane reaches 50 knots ground speed.

Interestingly, Boeing had already explored folding wingtips for the original 777 in the mid-1990s, even patenting a design. However, that version was heavy and complex; the technology only became commercially viable with the advancements in materials and actuation seen in the 777X. Combining advances in new material science with the newly acquired archives of McDonnell Douglas made it a natural evolution to develop the next-generation Boeing widebody with folding wings.

In its 1997 merger with McDonnell Douglas, Boeing inherited the F/A-18 Super Hornet program. The pivotal deal that integrated decades of naval aviation expertise into Boeing’s defense portfolio. By combining with the storied warplane manufacturer, Boeing inherited a rich legacy of naval fighter jet engineering and design. Looking past the hornet, the annals of the McDonnell portfolio include the most mass-produced supersonic naval fighter ever made, the F-4 Phantom II.

In naval aviation, wing folding is often a manual pilot action verified by ground crews. For the 777X, Boeing automated the process to reduce pilot workload: the wingtips automatically fold when ground speed drops below 50 knots after landing. Unlike the Super Hornet, where a significant portion of the wing folds, the 777X only folds the outer 3.5 meters (11 feet) of its tip. This minimizes the weight penalty and places the hinge where structural loads are lower compared to a mid-wing fold.

The 777X incorporates "spill-over" benefits from military R&D, specifically in the use of high-redundancy sensors and fail-safe locking pins that ensure the wing is structurally one piece before the engines can reach takeoff power. Boeing had to prove to the FAA that its new commercial mechanism could withstand aerodynamic loads equivalent to a fixed wing, leveraging testing methodologies honed over decades of military carrier operations.

In 1995, Boeing patented a design for folding wingtips on the original 777, but the proposal was abandoned because airlines rejected the idea. The primary reasons for its abandonment were the added weight, reduced fuel capacity, and increased maintenance costs associated with the design.

The main objective was to allow the widebody aircraft to fit into existing "Code E" airport gates, as initial designs anticipated a wingspan that might exceed standard limits. The original proposal featured a hinge positioned closer to the wing root, with the outer 21 feet (6.4 meters) of each wing designed to fold upward.

Airlines found the engineering solution overly complex. The hinge's location negatively affected fuel capacity and added significant structural weight, making the trade-offs in performance and cost unacceptable at the time. The concept was not entirely discarded and was later refined and implemented in the current Boeing 777X program, which features a much larger, more fuel-efficient carbon-fiber composite wing.

The folding mechanism on the 777X is placed further out on the wing, which minimizes the impact on fuel capacity and adds less weight than the 1995 design. The 777X's wingspan is significantly larger than the original 777 and would fall into the restrictive ICAO Code F category without the folding tips.

The 777X's 11-foot (3.36 meters) folding wingtips reduce the wingspan to within Code E limits when on the ground, allowing it to use most existing airport gates. This makes the aircraft more versatile and avoids costly airport infrastructure upgrades that competitors like the Airbus A380 require.

The main reason why Boeing wanted the merger and the decisions that led to the company's current state.

The 777X program is famously delayed by nearly a decade. Originally slated to debut in 2020 for launch customer Lufthansa, the enormous twinjet is not expected to enter full-rate production until 2027. Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said this year that the company has “a mountain of work” ahead of it for certification. These delays are in no small part due to the 737 MAX disasters, with two fatal crashes in 2018 and 2019 that caused the death of 350 Souls.

As the legendary American planemaker has course-corrected in the years following the tragic mishaps of the latest and greatest iteration of the 737, narrowbody mainline airliner, the 777X program has faced additional headwinds. The company refocused on quality control and pushed ahead to ensure that all airframes remain as high-quality as they have always been, since the days when passengers would say, "if it's not Boeing, I'm not going.”

The Dubai Airshow 2025 reaffirmed customer confidence in the 777X, as the colossal twinjet offers the only viable replacement for the world's aging fleets of jumbo jets, such as the Airbus A380 and the legacy Boeing 747. Emirates, which is the world's leading widebody operator, upped its order for 65 more of the forthcoming 777X. The aircraft promises to usher in a new era of commercial aviation, which we look forward to witnessing when the day comes.

#6140. Editorial: JetBlue Status Match Made Clear It’s Not For Me

Last June, JetBlue launched a status match that put elites from competing carriers into Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2. It also offered a faster track for Delta Diamond, Delta 360, AA Executive Platinum and Concierge Key members: earn 50 tiles by year-end and get Mosaic 4. That worked out to $5,000 in JetBlue flights or Paisly packages, or $50,000 on the JetBlue card, and a single Mint roundtrip to Europe could cover most of it. I already had AA Executive Platinum, so I didn’t need the status. I wanted it anyway. JetBlue was adding routes from my home airports, I fly to Boston, New York and Fort Lauderdale often, and the United partnership raised the possibility of benefits on both sides.

My application was approved just before the June 30 deadline. Some applicants waited up to six weeks for processing, though, and losing six weeks of a 12-week challenge is a real cost. JetBlue then added its 25-for-25 promotion on top. Visiting 25 destinations by year-end earned up to 350,000 TrueBlue points plus 25 years of Mosaic 1, which made a cheap, aggressive weekend of short hops look worth it. My plan was to finish the challenge through spend and put the points toward transatlantic and Japan trips. My one worry at the time was whether JetBlue would treat these new Mosaics well enough to keep them flying with it.

My two primary airports are Pittsburgh, PA (PIT) and Fort Myers, FL (RSW). I occasionally also fly from Fort Lauderdale or Miami when it makes sense. But Pittsburgh had just flights to Boston for some of last year, before adding Fort Lauderdale to fill the Spirit gap and then New York JFK competing with Delta, and more broadly to the New York market, United and American with more than enough flights. From Fort Myers, it’s Boston of JFK.

I flew once to Boston on JetBlue but at the time, it had not yet launched a domestic first class, a better seat selection included in my fare was the only real enhancement to the short flight of just over 80 minutes. I’ll cover other reasons why I wasn’t able to fly the carrier more, but given that I am not in New York, Boston, or Fort Lauderdale full time, every flight I take has a connection and it’s not particularly on-the-way for me. For example, if heading south to Florida, Charlotte, Atlanta, or even Washington Dulles make more sense than Boston or New York but when heading west at all, Chicago, Houston, Dallas, and Denver are all obviously better options.

Even to Europe, there’s not a material advantage with limited schedules and limited footprint on the continent. For trips to Paris given that I will have to connect anyway, I have more options on any other carrier through east coast hubs than with JetBlue on its metal not to mention partner networks.

Most recently, I had a flight to Cancun and with airport time, flight time and connections, it’s faster to fly out of Miami or Fort Lauderdale. But JetBlue had fewer flights for more money and far more miles than with American. Outside of the northeast corridor or based in South(east) Florida, I couldn’t make it make sense.

I’m heading to Europe for a meeting next week and I will finally have a chance to try Mint. This will constitute two of my longest flights with JetBlue ever. I haven’t heard many negative comments about JetBlue Mint, and I have high expectations. It’s hard to get excited about another American or United flight in business class solely because I have flown those so often and there’s little new there.

I’ll get a chance to try a reasonably long three-hour flight domestically to see how it differs from my prior JetBlue experience. Then, assuming flights are on time, I should have a chance to try the new BlueHouse, a first for me. Following that is a long haul flight in Mint and I am looking forward to the experience.

Statistically, I can’t see a reason that I try for Mosaic again, but who knows? The experience could change what appears to be a clear analytical decision for me at this point.

One of the biggest reasons I secure status via flying/spending/staying is to redeem systemwide upgrades (or suite upgrades in the case of hotels.) I’ll fully admit that upon receiving approval for the challenge last year, I hadn’t even considered that Mint certificates would work differently than other upgrade certificates in the industry. One upgrade certificate is worth an upgrade (if available.) United uses “Plus Points” but it feels clearer that there will be some variability in what’s required to move between the cabins.

For this particular trip, JetBlue wanted two upgrade certificates in one direction, and four on another. Thankfully, I had taken the upgrade option every time I achieved a choice to select a benefit, but had I chosen something else assuming that I’d only need two Move to Mint certificates (as I would with American for example) I would have come up short.

I covered how much spending is required to achieve top tier status and its associated benefits in recent posts. This was in response to United’s move to require $480,000 in annual spending (by credit card only) to achieve United 1K status. Assuming that along the way loyalty points are taken and annual Mosaic bonuses are applied to cardholders, JetBlue is above American at $225,000 in spend for Mosaic 4 vs. American’s net of $164,000 for Executive Platinum with just two systemwide upgrades, or $214,000 with six. The difference is that those six upgrades apply for the full-one-way on a single certificate.

I spent time trying to figure out why one way charged four Move to Mint vs two and in the end, it didn’t really matter. I can nearly upgrade my entire family of four on American vs a single roundtrip for myself. For what it’s worth, the base cost was also more expensive with JetBlue than American for which I had upgrades available.

I have the qualified business spend to earn Mosaic 4 every year, but the value of its perks aren’t even close to the rest of the market. And for what JetBlue expects in spend compared to what I could earn elsewhere is uncompetitive.

And as a side note, the fixed rate of JetBlue points (about 1.4¢/each) is unimpressive but for most of the attempts I tried to use them throughout the year both domestically and internationally, they proved of little value. A lack of partners is much the same. I looked at a redemption in Mint on my flights to Europe and though I had more than 220,000, it was an insufficient balance for the simple roundtrip. For context, I took United a few years ago on miles and redeemed 160,000 roundtrip (this year was available at 176,000 roundtrip) and multiple times in the last 24 months on American at or around 115,000 roundtrip. Miles aren’t worth enough, they aren’t flexible enough, and there aren’t enough partners to fill gaps in the JetBlue map.

I had higher expectations for JetBlue based on the experiences of my peers. I think its equipment is excellent, but widespread first class availability is a necessity. The limited utility of Move to Mint certificates were the nail in the coffin and the usability of the miles didn’t help. But even then, I really want to love and fly JetBlue, and I am willing to go a little out of my way to use them. But I’m not willing to fly backwards for fewer flights at a higher cost.

#6139. American’s Longtime Chief Operating Officer to Retire

American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom announced Friday.

Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

“He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

JonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

American will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A new reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be announced in December.

“For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

#6138. Air Canada Posted A Record $6.984 Billion Quarter While Its Basic Business Class Strips Out Flexibility & eUpgrades

Air Canada closed the third quarter of 2026 with record operating revenue of $6.984 billion, up 21% from the same period last year. The figure invites an easy narrative that the airline’s new Basic fares in business class and premium economy, introduced in late July, fueled the gain, but the evidence published so far does not support that conclusion.

A more useful question for travelers is what a Basic business ticket actually removes, and whether Air Canada’s version requires fewer sacrifices than those of Delta Air Lines and JetBlue, both of which have built similar premium tiers. Answering it requires looking first at what the quarterly results do and do not say, then at the fare rules themselves, and finally at how competing airlines have drawn the line between the seat and everything around it.

Passenger revenue reached roughly $6.3 billion, driven by yield up 11%, passenger load factor rising 2.6 percentage points to 89.1%, and cargo revenue growing 33%. Unit revenue climbed 14% on both a total and a passenger basis, a gain that arrived on top of capacity growth of 5.7%. Those figures describe an airline filling more seats at higher prices, a pattern consistent with a record quarter. All figures were reported by the airline.

Profitability told a different story, as fuel expense rose by $906 million while the price per liter climbed from 88.3 cents to 148.3 cents, and operating income slipped to $261 million from $284 million, compressing the operating margin to 3.7% from 4.9%. Adjusted EBITDA of $936 million landed slightly below last year’s $961 million, with the margin falling to 13.4% from 16.6%, while net income attributable to shareholders dropped to $139 million from $264 million and free cash flow turned negative by $440 million.

Prior Full-Year 2026 Guidance (Provided on August 11, 2026)

Management responded by lowering its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $2.4 billion to $2.7 billion, down from $2.9 billion to $3.2 billion, and attributed the change chiefly to higher expected fuel prices. The chief financial officer credited decisive pricing, capacity, and cost actions with softening the fuel impact, a phrase that describes recovering cost pressure rather than capturing premium leisure demand. Balance sheet actions continued alongside the operating results, as Air Canada used Aeroplan transaction proceeds to repay $1.7 billion of debt and completed an $800 million issuer bid that reduced shares outstanding by about 10%.

Executives reported that premium cabin revenue rose 19% and corporate revenue 22%, with North American markets posting the strongest unit revenue gains because shorter booking windows let the airline pass higher fuel costs into fares more quickly. Premium travel was already central to the airline’s economics, accounting for about 30% of passenger revenue in its 2025 results despite occupying far fewer seats than economy. The trend also predates the Basic launch, since premium revenue grew 11% in the second quarter, when no premium Basic fares existed.

Chief Commercial Officer Mark Galardo pointed to a behavioral shift, saying that premium customers, whether traveling for leisure or business, have been flying more in spring and autumn than during the summer peak. He described the quarter as a story of premium rather than budget passengers, and he predicted record September and October revenue. Galardo added that the shift began two or three years ago, has accelerated, and is now appearing slightly in November.

On the new fares, Galardo said in mid-August that it was far too early to judge reception because they had been on sale for barely more than a week, and he described United Airlines' early results with its own premium Basic fares as interesting. Because Air Canada’s Basic fares were on sale for only about the last nine weeks of a 13-week quarter, and because fuel-driven fare increases and shifting travel patterns were operating simultaneously, the sources reviewed provide no basis for crediting unbundling with the revenue gain.

In 2026, the airline has stopped flying to one long-haul city and five short-haul places. Find them all here!

Business Class Basic is sold on flights within Canada, to the United States, and to and from Central and South America, and it is not offered on long-haul itineraries such as Montreal to New Delhi. Tickets are non-refundable and carry no future travel credit, while changes up to two hours before departure cost $200 within Canada or to the US and $700 on international flights, in Canadian dollars. Same-day airport changes and standby are not permitted, advance seat selection carries a fee, and the checked allowance falls from two bags to one on Canada and US routes. Carry-on allowances remain at one personal article and one standard article across Basic, Standard, and Latitude.

Despite the cuts, the fare remains more than critics might expect, since passengers retain Maple Leaf Lounge access, priority check-in and baggage handling, and the same earning rate of one Aeroplan point and four Status Qualifying Credits per dollar. Premium Economy Basic is stricter because it drops lounge access, keeps the same flexibility limits, and, according to AwardWallet, excludes eUpgrade certificates. The business class table lists no eUpgrade row, which makes sense because no cabin sits above it, so the restriction mainly affects travelers who would otherwise apply certificates to a Premium Economy ticket. The savings are modest; on Toronto to Mexico City, AwardWallet found Basic at $1,022, Standard at $1,093, and Latitude at $1,256, leaving only a $71 gap between Basic and Standard, a spread that AwardWallet interprets as a nudge toward the pricier option.

Delta began selling Basic Business on July 8 for travel starting in September, and the fare preserves the lie-flat seat, Zone 1 boarding, and the standard Delta One meal while removing most of the ground experience. Seats are assigned after check-in, the checked allowance shrinks by one bag, and the ticket earns 2 SkyMiles per dollar instead of 5, although it still counts toward Medallion status. Delta also bars upgrades of every kind, paid ones included, and rules out same-day confirmed changes and standby. Delta First Basic has been flying since July in select domestic and Latin American markets, while Premium Select Basic follows alongside Basic Business in September.

Lounges mark the sharpest contrast, since Basic Business passengers keep Delta One check-in and the Delta One Lounge only through January 18, 2027, after which the privileges lapse unless obtained through a Sky Club membership or an eligible American Express card. Fees also differ, as AwardWallet reports that Delta raised the change and cancellation charge for Basic Business to $500 from $99 on travel originating in the United States and Canada, with cancellations yielding an eCredit toward a future ticket.

Measured against those terms, Air Canada’s version asks for less on several frontsbecause it retains lounge access, preserves full Aeroplan earnings, and charges $200 for changes within Canada or to the US, versus Delta’s $500. Its $700 international change fee, roughly US$496, is comparable to Delta’s, and its lack of any refund or credit is harsher than Delta’s eCredit. Air Canada also confines Basic to shorter routes, whereas Delta extends its premium Basic fares to select long-haul international markets.

As more and more airlines move unbundling further up the cabin, the carrier adds to this growing list.

JetBlue Airways sorts travelers first by onboard experience, choosing among Main, EvenMore, BlueFirst, and Mint, and then by up to three fare options named Base, Standard, and Flex that differ in seat selection and refundability. Base fares omit seat selection and return travel credit on cancellation, less any fee, and they are branded for Main, EvenMore, and BlueFirst. President Marty St. George framed the structure as two clicks: the onboard experience first and the fare second, according to the release.

The release states that Base fares are not available in Mint, so the lie-flat product keeps only its Standard and Flex tiers, and a Mint Base fare does not appear in JetBlue’s own description. BlueFirst, the domestic first-class product that begins rolling out later this year, is listed with a Base option, although JetBlue says fuller fare details will follow. United, which introduced unbundled premium fares in April 2026, and Lufthansa already sell comparable products, and Air Canada’s tiers resemble those of its partners.

The fourth-quarter report in early 2027 will be the first to cover a full quarter with Basic fares on sale, which should give analysts a cleaner view than the partial exposure in the third quarter. The reading will be clouded because Air Canada has said it is not yet providing 2027 guidance and has trimmed planned first-quarter 2027 capacity by two points; fuel prices remain the key variable in its outlook, and a new chief executive, Anko van der Werff, is due to arrive by the end of January 2027.

Within that noise, the most informative signal may be how many buyers choose Standard when the gap is as small as $71, a figure airlines rarely disclose that would show whether Basic is expanding the premium audience or repricing existing buyers. Delta’s lounge cutoff on January 19, will supply a parallel test of how travelers react to losing ground perks, and Air Canada, having kept its lounge access, can treat that contrast as either a selling point or a cushion for tightening its terms later. Because the incoming chief executive will inherit both the fare structure and the missing 2027 outlook, his first budget cycle may decide whether Basic remains a modest entry point or grows into the fare most travelers see first in search results.

#6137. The 7 Largest US Air Force Bases By Land Area

The USAF has some of the largest and most famous military bases anywhere in the world. But when it comes down to size, the question is which one is ultimately the largest of all the air bases. In this article, we are going to break down the seven biggest pieces of real estate owned by the USAF anywhere in the world.

As the largest air force of any military on the planet, the USAF not only has thousands of aircraft but also numerous ballistic missile sites and extensive facilities to support operations and logistics. Let's get down to it and go down the list, starting with the smallest entry first.

Fairchild AFB is located just southwest of Spokane, Washington. The base is a critical component of the Air Mobility Command and serves as one of the largest aerial refueling hubs in the USAF. The host unit, the 92nd Air Refueling Wing, operates a large fleet of KC-135 Stratotanker aircraft.

The base is also home to the Air Force's only Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape School. This facility trains roughly 20,000 students annually on how to survive being shot down and captured under the worst conditions possible.

The 36th Rescue Squadron supports both the SERE School and the entire Pacific Northwest region across a four-state area. The Air National Guard's 141st Air Refueling Wing and the Joint Personnel Recovery Agency, as well as an Armed Forces Reserve Center, are all located at Fairchild AFB.

Kirtland AFB is home to the nuclear command and Logistics arm of the Air Force Global Strike Command. The unit is a critical component of the US nuclear triad. The Space Force's Delta 15 is headquartered at Kirtland. The base is one of the largest employment sources in the state of New Mexico, with 20,000 personnel, including troops and civilians.

The base also hosts the Air Force Research Laboratory Directed Energy Directorate and the Space Vehicles Directorate. These units are focused on the development of advanced laser, microwave, and space-based technology.

The base supports over 100 mission partners and units. These include the Department of Energy's Sandia National Laboratories and Los Alamos National Laboratory, the Defense Nuclear Weapons School, and various Air National Guard and Reserve units.

Ten air force bases are listed as bases for the USAF F-35A, although they can operate from many more bases.

Edwards AFB is very deep in the Mojave Desert of Southern California, where it is home to around people doing some of the most advanced flight testing and research performed anywhere in the world. The base hosts the US Air Force Test Pilot School as well as NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center in the Air Force Research Laboratory. A number of government agencies and leading aerospace companies like Lockheed Martin, Boeing, and Northrop Grumman maintain permanent facilities on their campus.

Edwards is the headquarters for the Air Force Test Center. The bed of Rogers Dry Lake provides a 65-square-mile natural runway that offers a virtually perfect emergency landing area as well as a testing surface for many experiments. The base also has the largest anechoic chamber in the world for testing aircraft electronic and radio frequency systems.

Air Force Captain Chuck Yeager was the first human being to break the sound barrier when he flew the Bell X-1 rocket plane over the speed of sound at Edwards AFB in 1947. Since then, Edwards has been at the forefront of jet development, with the X-Plane series of increasingly faster supersonic prototypes being developed at the base.

The development of stealth technology also had its first steps at Edwards with the Lockheed Martin F-117 Nighthawk in the 1980s. Lockheed’s Skunk Works division also developed the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II at Edwards. Northrop Grumman tested the B-2 Spirit stealth bomber extensively at Edwards, and its successor, the B-21 Raider, is now flying over its airfield.

NASA and Lockheed are testing the X-59 QueSST (Quiet Supersonic Technology) at Edwards, which is working toward a low-boom design that will allow for renewed supersonic commercial aircraft development. It took its first flight at the end of October 2025. The base was even home to the NASA space shuttle program until 1991.

The USAF commands the world’s largest pilot corps — 14,486 strong — and here’s how many aircraft they fly and how to join their elite ranks.

Located in the northwest corner of Florida, dubbed the Panhandle, Eglin AFB is the primary test and evaluation center for all USAF weapons, navigation, and guidance systems. This installation hosts almost 20,000 military, civilian, and contractor personnel from the Air Force, Army, and Navy. The Space Force also has an AN/FPS-85 radar on the campus for space surveillance.

The Air Force Special Operations Command has a large presence on the base, including the Air Force's only Reserve Special Operations Wing, the 919th. The 33rd Fighter Wing is located on the base, which is a joint training unit for both pilots and maintainers of the Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II.

To facilitate the weapons-centric mission of Eglin AFB, the base manages a vast overwater range extending into the Gulf of Mexico. McKinley Climatic Laboratory tests aircraft and equipment under severe weather conditions, and the Air Force Research Laboratory's Munitions Directorate calls Eglin home as well.

Hill AFB manages the Utah Test and Training Range, which is a 1,490-square-mile expanse of desert used for testing and tactical training. Hill AFB is home to the first F-35 fighter wing that became operational in the USAF, the 388th Fighter Wing. The 75th Air Base Wing is responsible for running Hill AFB facilities.

The Ogden Air Logistics Complex at Hill AFB manages the life cycle sustainment of the Lockheed F-22 Raptor, F-35 Lightning II, F-16 Fighting Falcon, C-130 Hercules, and A-10 Thunderbolt II. The command is also responsible for the Minuteman III Intercontinental Ballistic Missile.

The 419th Fighter Wing of the US Air Force Reserve is also stationed at Hill AFB. The wing flies the F-16 'Viper,' as the jet is nicknamed, and deploys alongside active-duty units to support combat forces. As many as 20,000 troops and civilians work on the base to support the mission of all the different units stationed at Hill AFB.

The military transport suffered a midair catastrophe.

The Barry M. Goldwater Air Force Range is one of the premier military training ranges in the United States. The enormous base is used for realistic combat training, not only for US service branches, but also for allied partner nations' militaries. The vast expanse of the range allows for extensive real-world, live-fire air-to-air and air-to-ground tactical training. Around 15,000 people work at the range of the bases associated with it.

In addition to being instrumental as a joint forces, combined arms combat training facility, the base allows for advanced electronic warfare and other tactical scenarios. The range is jointly managed by both Luke AFB and Marine Corps Air Station Yuma. The Army National Guard also uses the range extensively. Almost all Marine Corps Aviation units train at this base before deployment to combat theaters.

Luke AFB is the primary fighter pilot training facility in the US Air Force. The base also recently transitioned to be the main training center for the F-35A Lightning II aircraft for both US pilots and pilots from any of the 19 other nations that also operate the Joint Strike Fighter, as the F-35 is also known. The base is home to the 56th Fighter Wing, which is the largest fighter wing in the USAF.

The former service personnel were flying to DC from Wisconsin for Veterans Day commemorations.

The main facility of Nellis AFB is situated in the northeastern corner of the Las Vegas Valley, hosting 15,000 troops and civilian staff. The base has long been a hub for advanced combat Aviation training. Every year, the International Air Warfare exercise known as 'Red Flag' is held at Nellis.

This airfield is home to the Air Force Warfare Center as well as the 99th Air Base Wing and the aerial demonstration team known as the Thunderbirds. The gargantuan military complex includes the Nevada Test and Training Range, Creech AFB, and the Tonopah Test Range (TTR).

In addition to hosting foreign Air Forces for joint training exercises, the base has a permanent presence of other services, including the Navy, Army, and Marine Corps. Sandia National Laboratories is also located on the base complex, within the boundaries of the TTR facility. NTTR encompasses approximately 3 million Acres of restricted airspace and land, which is home to the famed, highly classified Area 51 (Groom Lake), as well as the TTR.

These facilities have been instrumental in the development of iconic Advanced aircraft like the Lockheed U-2 Dragon Lady, SR-71 Blackbird, and F-117 Nighthawk. In addition to the Skunk Works projects, Area 51 hosts captured aircraft from adversaries that are reverse-engineered.

Sandia National Laboratories is part of the US Department of Energy. Its primary mission is to ensure the maintenance, security, safety, and reliability of the US nuclear weapons stockpile. The laboratory also contributes to the development of border security technology, renewable energy technology, missiles, advanced computing, satellites, and spacecraft.

Creech is located in Indian Springs, 45 miles north of the main base. It serves as a hub for the testing of remotely piloted aircraft and forthcoming collaborative combat aircraft. The vast expanse of the base exists as a safety buffer as well as a physical barrier that enhances the secrecy of the classified activities by leveraging simple geography.

The massive range includes numerous Military Operations Areas and Restricted Areas that are used for a myriad of military training activities as well as research and development. Aircraft, missiles, drones, and other weapon systems are all tested, developed, and stored within the grounds of Nellis AFB.

#6136. SFO’s Airfield Will Flood Amid Thanksgiving Rush With 9-Foot Tides Predicted, Officials Say

San Francisco International Airport (SFO) is facing a significant coastal flooding threat during one of the busiest travel periods of the year, with officials warning that exceptionally high tides could overwhelm vulnerable sections of its airfield. The National Weather Service (NWS) is forecasting water levels approaching nearly 10 feet or potentially higher around San Francisco Bay between Tuesday and Thursday, coinciding with the Thanksgiving travel rush.

Unusually high king tides, storm surge, warmer ocean temperatures, and an approaching winter storm are raising concerns about the airport's ability to keep its airfield and surrounding infrastructure clear of seawater. Although SFO is preparing for potential flooding, the situation could create additional complications for passengers, airlines, and airport operations during the holiday period.

According to the Los Angeles Times, both SFO and Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) are facing potential flooding as exceptionally high tides approach Northern California. NWS meteorologists warned of extreme coastal flooding along the San Francisco Bay shoreline, with water levels potentially exceeding nine feet depending on the storm surge. The forecast is concerning because SFO's seawalls are not uniformly high, leaving certain sections more vulnerable to overtopping.

According to Deep Arrival, NWS also warned that water levels along SFO's shoreline could reach approximately 9.9 feet (three meters) during the most concerning periods. The airport's seawall stretches for more than seven miles, but some vulnerable sections are reportedly only 8 feet high. The southeastern corner near Runway 28 Left is particularly exposed, while the northern ends of both runways also feature lower sections. It remains unclear whether the runways or taxiways themselves will experience flooding.

The airport is already preparing for the possibility of seawater entering its airfield. SFO spokesperson Doug Yakel said the airport was prepared to respond and maintain safe operations, according to Deep Arrival. Crews are clearing drainage areas, inspecting pump stations, and positioning sandbags and emergency flood barriers.

The flooding threat is being driven by several overlapping weather and astronomical factors. The NWS explains that unusually high king tides, thermal expansion from warmer ocean temperatures, and storm surge are combining to push bay water levels toward historic territory. According to its forecast discussion on Sunday, major to extreme coastal flooding is expected, with an impactful storm forecast to affect the region on Tuesday and Wednesday.

The NWS predicts the San Francisco tide gauge could reach 8.4 feet on Tuesday, and 8.6 feet (2.6 meters) on Wednesday, above mean lower low water. Thursday's predicted level is 8.2 feet (2.5 meters). These figures include the forecast tidal conditions, with additional storm-related water potentially worsening the situation. The previous record at San Francisco's Crissy Field gauge was 8.66 feet (2.63 meters), recorded in January 1983, according to the Los Angeles Times.

The implications extend beyond airport infrastructure. Highway 101, an important access route for SFO passengers, could also experience flooding, potentially making it difficult for travelers and airport employees to reach the terminals. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie has urged residents to avoid unnecessary journeys, particularly between Monday afternoon and Wednesday. The city is also suspending parking meter and time-limit enforcement during that period to help residents move their vehicles away from vulnerable areas, according to Deep Arrival.

The airport was the epicenter of a tremor less than two years ago.

The timing could hardly be worse for the airport, with Thanksgiving traditionally generating substantial domestic travel demand across the US. Any flooding affecting SFO's runways, taxiways, or surrounding access roads could complicate an already busy operating environment. However, officials have not confirmed that flight cancellations or runway closures will be necessary, and the airport is continuing its preparations to maintain safe operations.

OAK nearby is also monitoring the situation, although its infrastructure appears better positioned to withstand the predicted water levels. Deep Arrival reports that the airport has raised its perimeter dike to 13 feet (four meters), reaching 17 feet (five meters) in certain locations, and does not currently expect flooding. Meanwhile, the NWS anticipates drier conditions on Thanksgiving Day itself before another storm system potentially arrives during the following weekend.

Officials are urging passengers to monitor airline notifications and airport updates. The greatest concern is around late-morning high tides on Tuesday and Wednesday, when storm surge could push water beyond vulnerable seawall sections. Although flooding remains a forecast risk, not a confirmed operational disruption, the combination of high water levels and Thanksgiving passenger volumes presents a serious challenge for the airport and could disrupt travelers.

#6135. 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

Arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

Whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

If you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of big waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

Where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

Where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees

For a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

Where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

Where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a big fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees

The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

Where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

Though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend new heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

Where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees

December through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

Where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees

Another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

Where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees

Miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two important events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

Where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.

#6134. How to Spend 3 Perfect Days in Naples

A fascinating, complex, and multi-layered city, Naples is brimming with contradictions. Dilapidated, neglected neighborhoods share city space with splendid palaces and world-beating museums. The city’s origins go back to the ancient Greeks, yet the contemporary art scene here is buzzing. There is a state-of-the-art metro system designed by renowned artists and architects (no wonder, since the traffic is infamously heavy).

I’ve been visiting for over 30 years and have seen huge changes, most of them positive. Naples today is safer, more tourist-friendly, and cleaner than ever before, yet it remains Italy’s most beguiling city. The eating and drinking scene has evolved, there is a much wider choice of places to stay (with Rocco Forte due to open a hotel here in 2027), and museums and monuments have been spruced up and reorganized. In 2027, the America’s Cup will arrive as well.

You could easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything. But if you only have three days, start early and be prepared to pack in as much as possible; you can rest once you get home. Here is my advice for how to make the most of it.

You coudl easily spend two weeks in Naples and not see everything—but three days are a delicious taste, too.

Historic Gran Caffè Gambrinus is a perfect place to start your first day, shoulder to shoulder with the locals at the bar for a shot of espresso and a warm cornetto (only tourists sit on the terrace). Just across Piazza Trieste e Trento lies the imposing dark grey and red Palazzo Reale where you can visit the sumptuous Royal Apartments and ornate Teatrino, and on the other side is the Teatro San Carlo, one of Italy’s most prestigious opera houses; opera buffs can book a behind-the-scenes tour, or even better, tickets for a performance.

From the Toledo metro station, you get full immersion in the Stazione d’Arte, a public art project involving some of the greatest contemporary artists and architects who have transformed Naples’ main underground stations into public galleries. Dominated by Oscar Tusquets Blanca’s jaw-dropping mosaic, Toledo is one of the most impressive—but for just the price of a metro ticket (just over $2), you can tour them all.

A quick walk north on Via Toledo leads to Via della Pignasecca, where you can catch the end of the lively morning market with its troughs of slithering, glistening fish and seafood, piles of seasonal fruit and vegetables, and stalls selling everything from tripe to knock-off designer handbags.

Lunch at no-nonsense Trattoria da Nenella near Piazza Carità is a noisy, fun experience; you’ll probably have to queue, but the deep-fried anchovies and meatballs in tomato sauce are worth it, and prices are rock-bottom.

The Cappella Sansevero is home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

After a shot of the best coffee in the city at Café Mexico in Piazza Dante, you can spend the afternoon exploring the grid of streets around the so-called Spaccanapoli, the heart of Roman Neapolis where ancient monuments rub shoulders with street food stalls, tiny grocers, once-grand palazzi, and shops selling tourist trinkets and religious memorabilia. Piazza del Gesù, at the western end, is dominated by the eponymous church and an ornate roccoco ‘guglia’. Just to the east is the Church and Convent of Santa Chiara with a beautiful Gothic interior and a cloister famous for its bright, 18th-century majolica tiles. Close by is Naples’ most celebrated (and most crowded) sight, the Cappella Sansevero, home to Giuseppe Sammartino’s sublime 1753 marble Cristo Velato.

Back on the Spaccanapoli, nip into Gay-Odin (n. 61) for a chocolate gelato and then continue to the vast Duomo where you will be dazzled by the gilt-encrusted Cappella di San Gennaro and the subterranean church of Santa Restituita and its 4th-century baptistery.

Close by are the chapel of Pio Monte della Misericordia with Caravaggio’s seminal Seven Acts of Mercy and crumbling Piazza San Girolamini where Banksy’s Madonna with a Pistol appeared on the back right-hand wall in 2004. San Lorenzo Maggiore is an essential visit if you want to understand multi-layered Naples; under the 13th-century church, ongoing excavations have revealed the astonishing remains of a Greco-Roman city dating back 2,000 years.

A detour down Via San Gregorio Armeno takes you past shops selling pastori or figurines for Christmas cribs. Much of what you see is mass-produced these days, so for the real deal, visit Marco Ferrigno’s workshop at number 10. Continue to leafy Piazza Bellini, a lively evening hub, and bag a terrace table at Café Intramoenia for a Campari spritz—you’ve earned it.

For dinner, Europeo di Mattozzi is a personal favorite for its echoes of elegant old Naples; the classic food is fantastic (try the sublime melanzane alla parmigiana and the pasta with potatoes and provola cheese), the host Alfonso is charming, and your fellow diners are likely to be mostly locals.

Use Castel dell'Ovoa as your launchpad for a classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag.

Day two starts where it all began. Parthenope—later Neapolis and later still Napoli—was founded more than 2,500 years ago on the tiny island of Megaris, now occupied by the Castel dell’Ovo and the picturesque fishing hamlet of Borgo Marinari. There’s nothing much to see in the castle, but it’s a good launch pad for the classic Neapolitan passeggiata along the wide, traffic-free seafront drag. It’s lined with restaurants and cafés offering tables in the sun for a cappuccino and magnificent views.

The delightful neighbourhood of Chiaia is a criss-cross of pretty cobbled lanes peppered with independent boutiques, cool bars, and tiny restaurants; Via dei Mille and Via dei Filangeri are known for designer clothes and chic galleries. The handmade silk ties at tiny, old-fashioned Marinella make wonderful gifts, and a counter perch at tiny Pescheria Mattiucci is a good choice for a quick seafood lunch with a glass of something chilled and white.

Depending on the weather (and energy levels), one option from here is to head west beyond Mergellina to the upmarket seaside suburb of Posillipo for an afternoon on the beach; sunbeds and umbrellas can be rented at Bagno Sirena.

Or you can hop on the Funicolare di Chiaia and trundle up to leafy Vomero and the panoramic Certosa di San Martino, a Carthusian monastery complex with an ornate church, several museums, two cloisters, and the famous Monk’s Cemetery decorated with marble skulls. It also has knock-out views over the whole waterfront and the Bay of Naples to the Sorrentine Peninsula. The Friggitoria Vomero—one of the city’s few remaining authentic ‘frying shops’—doles out sizzling snacks from 6 p.m. and is conveniently close to the funicolare stop as you head back down the hill.

Chiaia’s quiet lanes morph into a nightlife hub from aperitivo hour on, filling up with smartly dressed locals and visitors in search of a good night out. Cocktail spot per eccellenza is retro-glam Antiquario where the jacketed barmen mix a stonking Negroni. From here it’s a short stroll to tiny Ristorante Dora, open since 1973, for textbook versions of fish and seafood classics such as spaghetti alle vongole (with local clams). Head back to Chiaia for a nightcap; follow your nose and the party crowd.

The atmospheric burial site of Cimitero delle Fontanelle is a respite from the buzzing streets above.

A no-go area for tourists until relatively recently, the dilapidated, densely populated but intriguing Rione Sanità is Naples in the raw. Breakfast at Pasticceria Popella in Via Arena alla Sanità is a must for their sfogliatelle and cream-stuffed ‘fiocchi di neve’ before having a rummage among the market stalls and tiny shops on Via dei Vergini; at n. 19 is the grand entrance to the famous pale green and cream Palazzo dello Spagnuolo with its celebrated ‘flying staircase’ by local architect Ferdinando San Felice.

These shambolic streets are filled with tooting cars, buzzing vespas, and bewildered tourists, but there are hidden artistic gems too: the 2,400 year-old recently restored Ipogeo dei Cristallini, the atmospheric burial site of the Cimitero delle Fontanelle with its piles of skulls and bones; and the labyrinthine Catacombs of San Gaudioso under the basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità.

You can’t visit the Sanità without a meal at Ciro Oliva’s crazy-lively temple to pizza Concettina ai Tre Santi (booking is essential), where the tasting menus offer an endless succession of slices topped with whatever the pizzaiolo dreams up at the time.

Naples’ Archaeological Museum (aka Mann) houses one of the world’s great collections of ancient art and artefacts, and if you only visit one museum, make it this. Must-sees include the monumental Roman sculptures on the ground floor, the collection of ancient erotica in the Gabinetto Segreto, and the dazzling mosaics, wall paintings, and bronzes from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

Afterwards, check out the brilliant selection of exquisite handmade gloves at factory prices in the workshops of Omega, a family glove business that first opened in 1923, before winding up the day in the surprisingly peaceful oasis of the exotic Orto Botanico gardens on traffic-clogged Via Foria.

For a last blast, Grand Hotel Parker’s on the way up to Vomero is the smart place to go. Cocktails and light bites are served on the rooftop terrace while on the floor below, chef Domenico Candela whips up a storm with his two-Michelin-star take on local cuisine to a backdrop of unforgettable views.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6133. Livery of the Week: Iberia’s Red-and-Yellow Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

The airline unveiled its new corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

The most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

Iberia’s new branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

The redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

The first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

Iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

The current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

Iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.
