#6132. How Much Narrower Economy Seats Get When Airlines Fly 10-Abreast Cabins

The discussion of how narrow economy-class seats are when fitted 10-abreast vs. nine-abreast is largely restricted to the Boeing 777 and Airbus A350. These two aircraft cabins are sized so that they are variously configured nine-abreast or 10-abreast. The massive A380 was wide enough so that it was only fitted with 10-abreast economy seating. Nine-abreast was unnecessary for the Superjumbo, even for premium-heavy mainline carriers, while regulations preclude any consideration of 11-abreast configuration.

The A330 (including A330neo) and Boeing 787 airliners are typically nine-abreast aircraft, although some earlier mainline Boeing 787s were configured eight-abreast in economy. Today, Japan Airlines remains the only airline to configure its flagship Dreamliners eight-abreast. The A330 and 787 are not realistically wide enough for a 10-abreast configuration.

Both the Boeing 777 and the Airbus A350 were originally designed for nine-abreast seating. The Boeing 777 was developed as a luxury long-haul aircraft that would offer relatively generous seat width with a 3-3-3 layout. This made it one of the more comfortable high-capacity widebodies. The original 777s came with an internal cabin width of around 19 feet, 3 inches (5.87 meters). They were all configured nine-abreast.

Later, Boeing 777-200LRs and -300ERs widened this to 19 feet, 3 inches (5.86 meters). The A350 followed almost two decades after the 777 originally entered service and followed a similar philosophy. But while it was called the 'Xtra Wide Body' (XWB), Airbus trimmed its width relative to the Triple Seven. Its width was considered spacious enough for a comfortable nine-seat economy configuration.

These Airbus A350s were built with an internal cabin width of 18 feet, 5 inches (5.60 meters). The old-production standard A350s were wider than the early Boeing 777s, but they also came at a later time when pressures for denser seating had increased. All these aircraft were physically and legally capable of fitting ten abreast (3-4-3), but airlines chose not to.

As a rule of thumb, low-cost airlines concentrate on regional travel with the Boeing 737 and Airbus A320 families. Long-haul international routes have been the domain of mainline carriers. Low-cost carriers work in a market segment that pushes for denser seating to reduce the cost per seat. Meanwhile, mainline carriers put more emphasis on premium seating and their premium brands. However, some low-cost carriers have moved into the long-haul leisure route market segment.

The two sister low-cost, long-haul, leisure airlines, Air Caraïbes and French Bee, have both purchased fleets of A350s. These are original production A350s, and both use the 3-4-3 (10-abreast) economy seating layout. This allows Frenchbee to achieve the A350-1000's maximum certified seat count of 480 (40 premium and 440 economy). Air Caraïbes also has the same configuration on some of its A350-1000s.

The result is rather squishy. The published seat width for these economy seats is around 16 inches (41 cm). For reference, the industry average across the airline industry for economy class seats is 17 to 18 inches (about 43–46 cm). These two low-cost airlines are the only ones to have configured their old production A350s in this way. They can because their marketing is not so much concerned with onboard comfort; it's about getting passengers to far-flung leisure destinations as cheaply as possible. Just endure the flight.

The changes to the A350's interior, and the impact this could have on the market.

Historically, airlines configured their Boeing 777-200LRs and 777-300ERs nine-abreast (3-3-3), giving economy class passengers 18–18.5 inches (46–47 cm) in seat width. At the same time, market forces increasingly favored a high-density economy-class cabin. This generation of 777 was around four inches (nine cm) wider than the older aircraft.

Today, most of the world's 777-300ERs have been fitted or retrofitted to seat 10-abreast, cutting the seat width to approximately 17 inches (43 cm). Some carriers have resisted the trend, notably Japan Airlines, ANA, Korean Air, and Singapore Airlines. But most, including premium-branded airlines like Qatar and Emirates, are now 10-abreast.

But even with the nine-abreast hold-outs, it has sometimes not been for the want of trying. In September 2025, Korea's JoongAng reported, "Korean Air is reconsidering its plan to change the seating layout in economy class from a “3-3-3” to a tighter “3-4-3” arrangement after a mounting backlash from consumers." Korean Air has not yet published a final seat map or official cabin configuration for its ordered Boeing 777-9 aircraft, but it would be surprising if it retains the nine-abreast configuration.

At 19 feet, 7 inches (5.97 meters), the 777-300ER was already wide enough for most mainline carriers to configure economy class 10-abreast. The incoming Boeing 777-9 and 777-8 (777X) come with thinner walls, allowing them to have a cabin width of 19 feet, 7 inches (5.97 meters). Boeing actively trolls Airbus and its A350, saying on its 777X product page, "Up to 40 cm (16 inches) wider than the A350."

The extra width will give the remaining holdout airlines more freedom to opt for the denser layout. ​​​​​In November 2026, Singapore Airlines announced its new 777-9 cabin with 17.6 inches (44.7 cm) for economy seats in a 3-4-3 configuration. The 777-9's cabin is wider and longer than the 777-300ER, but this will not necessarily increase the aircraft's density, as the vast majority of 777-300ERs are already 10-abreast. Ironically, the opposite is almost true because other market forces are pushing for more premium seating.

The Boeing 777-300ER is certified to carry up to 550 passengers in an ultra-high density layout. The 777-9 has more cabin space to fit even more seats, but Boeing is limiting its maximum exit-limit seat count by 75 seats (to 475) or by 110 seats (to 440), depending on the door configuration. Put another way, the 777-9 is envisioned to have more business and premium economy seats, while the already standard 10-abreast economy will benefit from a few more inches of lateral space. The economy class cabin is expected to shrink.

Ryanair is notable for asking Boeing to build a specific MAX 8 variant for high-density seating, while others configure A350s ten-abreast.

As stated, the old production A350s have an internal cabin width of approximately 18 feet, 5 inches (5.60 meters). Without introducing a new variant or generation, Airbus introduced a new production standard that increases the usable cabin length and thins the aircraft walls. This allows the new-production standard cabin width to be 18 feet, 9 inches (5.72 meters). The first new-production standard A350s were delivered in 2022.

For airlines retaining the nine-abreast seating, it allows the typical economy seat width to grow from approximately 18 inches (46 cm) up to 18.7 inches (47.5 cm). That will be welcome to passengers. However, it also made 10-abreast seating more feasible. These new aircraft with 10-abreast seating can accommodate 17-inch (43 cm) seats, bringing it closer to the conventional industry standard for economy seating.

To date, Philippine Airlines appears to be the only mainline carrier to opt for 10-abreast economy on new production standard A350s. It is able to offer up to an inch more in seat width than French bee, but also has to trim more than an inch relative to airlines operating the A350 in nine-abreast. With the airline industry being a game measured in a couple of marginal inches and pressure for dense economy seating, it's possible more carriers will follow suit.

The Boeing 777 was originally designed as a nine-abreast airliner, but it has since grown by eight inches (17 cm) in cabin width over its life. This has allowed it to transition to a 10-abreast airliner without having to sacrifice much of its original spaciousness. The original economy class seats were around 18–18.5 inches (46–47 cm), and the next generation is expected to be around 18 inches (46 cm). This may not be an improvement for economy class passengers, but it is not catastrophic either.

The A350 echoes the 777's path, while also being much more constrained. The A350 can be and is configured 10-abreast, but this reduces the seat width to 16–17 inches (41-43 cm). But there is also some degree of an apples-to-oranges comparison here. For economy passengers, the 777-9 doesn't normally have the advantage. They will be configured 10-abreast, while the A350 is almost always nine-abreast.

The new-production-standard nine-abreast A350 has a meaningful advantage of approximately 1.1 inches (2.8 cm), or 6.25% more seat width per economy passenger compared with a 10-abreast 777-9. This A350's nine-abreast vs. the 777X's 10-abreast comparison is important as it's a better representation of the actual industry standard. It's also worth noting that the A350 is more versatile than the 777X in terms of its missions and airlines. Only a relatively limited number of mainline carriers are purchasing the 777X, while a larger range of airlines, including low-cost airlines, are purchasing (often smaller) A350 fleets.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6130. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6129. Unresponsive Cessna Prompts Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 TCAS Alert Over Palm Springs

An Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alert after encountering an unresponsive Cessna while climbing out of Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) last week. AC1769, bound for Vancouver International Airport (YVR), reportedly received a resolution advisory at approximately 11,400 feet, prompting its pilots to climb to 12,000 feet to avoid the nearby aircraft. The incident occurred shortly after the aircraft departed Palm Springs, with the smaller aircraft reportedly failing to respond.

Although the encounter triggered an automated collision-avoidance warning, the Air Canada aircraft continued its scheduled journey without diverting or returning to the airport. The 737 MAX 8 subsequently landed safely in Vancouver. While the incident highlights the importance of onboard collision-avoidance technology, several details surrounding the encounter, including the Cessna's identity and the minimum distance between the two aircraft, remain unknown.

According to AIRLIVE, AC1769 departed Palm Springs International Airport at 12:45 PM local time on November 17. The aircraft, registered C-FSDB, was a 737 MAX 8 operating a scheduled service to Vancouver. It departed from Runway 31R and began its climb towards cruising altitude when its onboard Traffic Collision Avoidance System detected potentially conflicting traffic.

The reported encounter involved a small Cessna that was not responding as the Canadian aircraft climbed through approximately 11,400 feet. The TCAS resolution advisory instructed the Air Canada pilots to climb to 12,000 feet, representing an additional 600 feet of altitude. This maneuver was intended to establish greater vertical separation between the two aircraft and resolve the potential traffic conflict.

Importantly, the reported alert was a resolution advisory (RA), not a proximity warning. According to AeroSillage, an RA provides pilots with instructions to modify or maintain their vertical flight path to address a potential collision threat. The available reports do not establish the exact distance between the aircraft when the alert occurred.

TCAS is an important layer of aviation safety, particularly when aircraft encounter potentially conflicting traffic in busy airspace. The technology uses information transmitted by nearby aircraft transponders to identify potential collision threats. Depending on the circumstances, the system can issue traffic advisories or resolution advisories, recommending that pilots climb or descend to increase vertical separation.

Unlike instructions from air traffic controllers, TCAS resolution advisories are generated automatically using onboard surveillance equipment. According to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual, pilots are expected to follow an RA promptly unless doing so would jeopardize the aircraft's safety. However, the circumstances surrounding the Cessna's reported lack of response remain unclear. AeroSillage noted that the available reporting does not establish whether the smaller aircraft failed to answer a radio communication or did not comply with an air traffic controller's instruction. Its registration, the nature of the communication attempts, and the minimum separation between the aircraft have not been disclosed.

A private aircraft made an unexpected turn, putting it on a course to collide with the inbound American Airlines aircraft.

Despite the reported encounter, AC1769 continued its journey to Canada without an emergency diversion. AIRLIVE reported that the aircraft landed at Vancouver International Airport at 4:45 PM local time, completing the approximately two-hour-and-40-minute journey. Flight-tracking information independently confirms that this 737 MAX 8 operated the Palm Springs-Vancouver service and reached its destination. No other details or further emergency involving the aircraft were reported. Nevertheless, the incident illustrates how unexpected traffic conflicts can require immediate action even during otherwise routine departures.

Based on available reporting, no specific findings from the US or Canadian authorities have established the circumstances of the encounter. Without an official reconstruction, it remains impossible to determine whether the Cessna experienced a communication problem, whether an instruction was missed, or how close the aircraft actually came.

#6126. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

#6125. The Aircraft Set To Replace British Airways’ Boeing 777-200ERs At London Heathrow

British Airways (BA) is about to retire the aircraft that built its long-haul network, but it has not told anyone exactly what will take its place at London Heathrow (LHR). The airline’s 43 Boeing 777-200ERs average roughly 26 years of age, according to Aerospace Global News, and most of them fly from Heathrow rather than Gatwick. The one firm date BA has given belongs to the other London airport: in a February 27, 2026 message to colleagues, CEO Sean Doyle said the first new Boeing 787-10 will be delivered to Gatwick in 2029, as published by the British Airways Media Centre.

So what is actually coming for Heathrow’s 777-200ERs? Two types dominate the picture: the Airbus A350-1000, which is already stepping onto some of that flying, and the Boeing 787-10, with the long-delayed Boeing 777-9 expected to follow. One caveat before going further. BA has published neither a retirement date nor a route-by-route replacement plan for Heathrow, so every swap beyond Nashville described below is a possibility. The first real clue, though, arrived from the home of country music, and it hints at a bigger shift than a simple like-for-like swap. Read on, because the answer may change which jet you board on your next transatlantic trip.

Gatwick (LGW) is the easiest part of the puzzle to understand because BA has actually given it a delivery date. Aerospace Global News, citing Cirium data, reported that BA served 13 destinations from Gatwick in March 2026, all lower-yielding leisure flights, from Antigua and Cancun to Orlando and Mauritius, plus Accra and Islamabad for visiting-friends-and-relatives traffic. The same outlet notes that around 12 aircraft are typically based there and that some suggest 17 could be once the 787-10 arrives. The new jets are not expected to have a First cabin. The outlet also suggests that a larger Gatwick presence could make the airport more attractive to oneworld partner airlines hoping to feed connecting passengers into BA’s network.

There is also a technical twist. According to Turning Left For Less, BA’s earliest 787-10s lacked crew rest bunks and were range-limited, so the newly ordered aircraft will get an increased-gross-weight modification and bunks. The site lists Vancouver, Phoenix, Mauritius, Cancun and Las Vegas as routes that become workable. BA's newly ordered Boeing 787-10s will be powered by General Electric GEnx engines, following the airline's decision to introduce a second engine supplier alongside Rolls-Royce on its Dreamliner fleet. Doyle’s own message confirmed the bunks, and Aerospace Global News adds that the rest areas should be welcome news for crew, since the airline’s initial 787-10s do not have them.

That gives BA a relatively clean renewal path at LGW. Heathrow is harder. Most of the 43 777-200ERs are still tied to the airport, and replacing a four-class, business-heavy aircraft with a 787-10 without First would change the product as well as the capacity. Yet one Heathrow route has already provided a much more interesting clue.

The Airbus A350-1000 is not merely a future possibility at Heathrow. As reported by Simple Flying, BA scheduled the A350-1000 to replace the 777-200ER on its daily Heathrow–Nashville service from March 29, based on schedule data first spotted by Ishrion Aviation. Published flight times stay at 9 hours 10 minutes outbound as BA223 and 8 hours 10 minutes back as BA222, although the A350 cruises slightly faster than the 777. In winter, the route has used the Boeing 787-8, and the report says there is no word yet on whether that aircraft returns once the cold season arrives.

Simple Flying's database shows the Heathrow 777-200ER on this route seats 272 passengers, while the A350-1000 seats 331, a jump of 59. The seat models are the same, but Simple Flying notes BA fits a smaller galley area to squeeze in the extra rows, and Turning Left For Less says cabin crew have voiced concern about galley space on the type.

Seat counts on Heathrow–Nashville, per aeroLOPA data cited by Simple Flying.

Economy passengers may even gain a little comfort, since the A350 has one fewer seat per row than the 777. But the strategic point is bigger: BA added 59 seats to a route without adding a single flight. Why would an airline do that, and what does it say about the rest of Heathrow’s fleet? There is also a cargo angle. Simple Flying points out that the A350-1000 is comparable in size to the Boeing 777-300ER and so has a significantly larger hold, which on a short transatlantic sector lets BA load more freight than before.

A look at the changes coming to this route and what it means.

Because Heathrow is the one airport where BA cannot simply add flights. Writing in 2023, when the airline was still weighing its options, One Mile At A Time argued that Heathrow is capacity-controlled and that the larger A350-1000 and 787–10 variants offer excellent economics. They also noted that BA’s 777 fleet averaged nearly 20 years of age at the time, with nearly two-thirds of the jets delivered in 2001 or earlier, mostly the 777-200ER variant. Aerospace Global News makes a similar point about Gatwick: basing new jets there relieves pressure on a heavily slot-constrained Heathrow hub.

Efficiency is the other half of the logic. According to Airbus, the A350 Family delivers a 25% advantage in fuel burn, operating costs and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation competitor aircraft. That improvement comes from combining advanced aerodynamics, new-generation Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and lightweight materials, which account for more than 70% of the airframe. For BA, this makes the A350-1000 particularly attractive at a slot-constrained airport such as Heathrow: it can carry more passengers on an existing departure while benefiting from the efficiency gains of a newer-generation design.

That combination of capacity and efficiency helps explain why BA has ordered more than one type of new-generation widebody rather than choosing a single replacement for every 777. The order book tells the story. BA has 24 Boeing 777-9s on order after adding six aircraft in March 2025. It has also ordered six additional A350-1000s and 38 Boeing 787-10s, including the 32-aircraft order announced in 2025.

Those numbers make one aircraft particularly important. Twenty-four 777-9s are supposed to become BA's largest new-generation widebodies, but none has yet joined the fleet. The timing of that arrival could determine how quickly the oldest Heathrow 777s can finally disappear.

The 777-9 is the biggest aircraft in BA's replacement plan, and it is also the one that introduces the most uncertainty. We reported in August 2026 that the aircraft was still working through the tail end of its certification sequence as of mid-2026. In a November piece, we added that Boeing is expected to deliver its first 777-9 in 2027, by which time Airbus will likely have well over 150 A350-1000s flying.

For BA, Turning Left For Less expects a four-class layout of eight First, 65 Club Suites, 46 World Traveller Plus and 206 economy seats, 325 in all, debuting from 2027 or 2028 with the airline’s new First suite. Against the A350-1000’s 331 seats, the 777-9 would not even add capacity on a Nashville-type route, which complicates the idea of the 777-9 as a simple 777-200ER successor.

The same site expects the new First suite to be limited to the 24 Boeing 777-9s and the 12 refurbished Airbus A380s, which would make the 777-9 as much a flagship statement as a fleet-replacement tool.

Until the 777-9 shows up, the old jets keep flying, and flying hard, with most replacements still years away. What does that wait mean for passengers boarding one tomorrow?

Ten classic airliners relied on a third cockpit crew member, but their reasons for doing so reveal how dramatically commercial aviation evolved.

That leaves BA with an awkward transition period. Turning Left For Less says BA intends to retire all 43 777-200ERs, some of which will exceed 30 years of age by withdrawal, and its reader analysis suggests the last four, delivered in 2009, could stay longer because they are younger. BA has confirmed none of that beyond Doyle’s statement about Gatwick. Put differently, the exit date for the oldest airframes is still a matter of informed speculation, not a published schedule.

The wait has had visible moments. FlyMag reported that BA229 to Baltimore returned to Heathrow on July 9, 2026, and BA183 to New York turned back the next evening, both operated by 777-200ERs after crews identified technical issues, and both flights were subsequently canceled. Age alone is not proof of unreliability, since many 777s worldwide have flown happily for decades, but the incidents landed just as the renewal timeline moved into focus.

Every extra month of waiting sharpens the question BA has so far left unanswered in public: which Heathrow route loses its 777-200ER next, and will passengers on it get a First cabin back? The answer may arrive route by route, in schedule filings, long before any formal announcement.

Two milestones will settle how this plays out, and neither is fully in BA’s hands. The first is the pace of 787-10 deliveries after the Gatwick debut in 2029. The second is whether Boeing can certify and hand over the 777-9 on the schedule it now promises. If the Dreamliners flow, BA can retire 777-200ERs without leaving Heathrow gaps. If the 777-9 slips again, the A350-1000 is the obvious stopgap, yet the six additional aircraft on order are a modest cushion.

There is a premium-cabin cost to watch as well. Turning Left For Less points out that the new First suite does not fit four abreast in a 787 and that the A350-1000 carries no First at all, so some Heathrow routes could lose the cabin entirely as the 777-200ERs go. That is precisely the trade-off BA has not yet explained to the customers paying for it. Some will welcome newer jets with quieter cabins and more consistent Club Suites; others will see a quiet downgrade of the flagship experience at the airport where BA charges its highest fares.

One Mile At A Time wrote a 2023 article saying they were curious about how it would all play out. Three years on, the cast is clear, but the final act is not. So what do you think: should BA hold on to its youngest 777-200ERs until the 777-9 arrives, or are the A350-1000 and 787-10 enough on their own? Tell us in the comments, and let us know which Heathrow route you would like to see upgraded first.

#6123. Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson fights to stay on 2027 ballot amid City Hall exodus, credit warning

Johnson, Tobin reports, could be kicked off the ballot for re-election.

Democratic Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson is fighting to keep his name on the 2027 ballot with his administration is engulfed in a fiscal and leadership meltdown at City Hall.

Election officials are reviewing challenges to more than 25,000 of Johnson's nominating signatures ahead of the Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral election, a threshold fight unfolding just days after his third chief financial officer in 10 months abruptly resigned, Standard & Poor's placed Chicago's credit rating on negative watch and the City Council voted 45-5 to investigate three years of city financial reporting for possible misstatements.

Despite the mounting pressure, Johnson brushed off questions about whether he will survive the ballot challenge.

"Yeah, feeling just fine. I'm going to be on the ballot," Johnson told ABC 7 Chicago about the challenge. "Looking forward to building the safest, most affordable big city in America, and we're going to continue to do that work."

CHICAGO'S 12-LANGUAGE BALLOTS MAKE ELECTIONS 'HARDER TO MONITOR,' ILLINOIS GOP CHAIR WARNS

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks to demonstrators in Grant Park who were protesting the policies of President Donald Trump and showing their support for union labor on May 1, 2025, in Chicago. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Johnson needs 12,500 valid signatures to qualify for Chicago's Feb. 23, 2027, mayoral ballot. Hearing officers at the Chicago Board of Elections are reviewing more than 25,000 signatures challenged by supporters of perennial mayoral candidate Willie Wilson.

Johnson's campaign says 6,718 signatures were not challenged and projects that he would finish with 14,788 valid signatures if the first day's 32% validation rate holds. That would put him 2,288 signatures above the requirement, but the figure is the campaign's estimate, not a final board tally. The objectors say early rulings are favoring their challenge, and the review remains unresolved.

The turmoil inside City Hall accelerated after the sudden departure of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch, who said continuing in the role would "compromise my integrity and professional obligations." Johnson later said she "wasn't the right fit."

"It’s yet another high-level change in the mayor’s administration and is a sign of continuing turmoil and a lack of direction at a very key time for the city, especially for him heading into a mayoral election," David Greising, CEO of the Better Government Association, told CBS Chicago after Gabrysch's abrupt exit.

A survey of 1,108 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago, conducted Sept. 13-23, found that 22.2% approved of Johnson's job performance, while 52.9% disapproved and 24.8% had no opinion. The survey predates both the current petition review and Gabrysch's departure.

4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS

Chicago residents are calling for more police as crime continues to rise in the Windy City. (Fox News Digital)

Johnson's proposed $17.6 billion 2027 budget is intended to close an $882.4 million gap, but a 28-member City Council bloc told him it did not see the votes needed to pass his tax proposals.

Standard & Poor's ultimately placed Chicago's BBB general-obligation rating on negative CreditWatch, citing the budget stalemate and management instability. The agency said there was at least a 50% chance of a downgrade within 90 days, which could raise the city's borrowing costs.

The City Council eventually voted 45-5 on Wednesday to authorize an independent review of three years of financial reporting for possible material or intentional misstatements.

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson speaks during a news conference March 25, 2026, in Chicago (AP Photo/Erin Hooley)

Fox News Digital reached out to Mayor Brandon Johnson's office and campaign, the Chicago Board of Elections and Christopher Berry, a University of Chicago professor and faculty director of the Mansueto Institute for Urban Innovation, which commissioned the ChicagoSpeaks survey conducted by NORC. They did not respond by publication.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

#6122. American Grows Maintenance Footprint in Miami

A new deal with Miami-Dade County will help American Airlines solidify and eventually expand its maintenance operations at Miami International Airport.

The county announced this week that it will buy a hangar and maintenance space at Miami International from a third-party owner and lease it directly to American for its MRO operations. The acquisition includes Hangar 890, Building 891, 10.2 acres of land, and a 2.2-acre parking lot.

According to the Miami Herald, American already leases the property and uses it for maintenance work, but a change in ownership from private jet operator Aero Miami to the county will give American more leeway to develop the space as it sees fit. The new lease with the county will run for 20 years and cost American $67.8 million, the newspaper said.

The airline plans to keep more than 650 aircraft maintenance workers at the facility. It has also agreed to complete about $13.9 million in building repairs.

“Miami is a cornerstone of American’s international network and a consequential part of our long-term growth strategy,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “This agreement reinforces our dedication to our Miami team and preserves our ability to continue growing our network to more destinations around the world for our customers.”

American is the largest airline at Miami, carrying more than half of all passengers there.

#6121. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6120. Is Qantas Really Replacing Its Boeing 737-800s With Airbus A321XLRs Built For Longer Routes?

Is Qantas really replacing its Boeing 737-800s with Airbus A321XLRs built for longer routes? For travelers across Australia and beyond, such a decision greatly impacts how Qantas plans to run its busiest domestic corridors and regional gateways over the next decade. The airline's 737 fleet carries nearly half of all passengers Qantas flies each year, so any shift in the aircraft replacing those jets carries major consequences for flight frequency, onboard comfort, and airline profitability.

That transition sits inside Project Winton, Qantas' fleet renewal program that leads a decisive pivot from Boeing narrowbodies toward Airbus aircraft alongside Airbus A220s for QantasLink. So what is Qantas planning, and how could this move set the airline up for a decade of dominance?

Qantas is replacing its Boeing 737-800s with the Airbus A321XLR, even though the vast majority of its A321XLRs fly domestic sectors rather than the long-range missions the aircraft was designed to serve. Instead of reserving the extra-long-range narrowbody strictly for distant international flying, Qantas is leaning on the A321XLR as its main high-capacity domestic replacement for its aging 737-800 fleet across Australia's busiest trunk corridors.

Qantas' commitment to the A321XLR expanded steadily as fleet renewal requirements evolved. What started as an initial plan for at least 20 A321XLRs grew to 28 aircraft, and in August 2025 Qantas ordered 20 more A321XLRs to accelerate 737 retirements, bringing its total A321XLR order to 48 jets. Stepping up the order count gives Qantas deeper replacement capacity as older single-aisle airframes reach retirement age, and demand remains strong across major domestic city pairs.

Deliveries and early fleet withdrawals have already moved into active operations. Qantas took six A321XLRs during its 2026 financial year ahead of 737 fleet retirements beginning in late 2026, while signing a seven-year agreement to sell 44 737-800s and 88 CFM56-7B engines to AerFin, with initial aircraft exits already underway in late 2026, as per AeroMorning. Together, early arrivals and initial retirements mark the start of a multi-year transition away from Qantas' Boeing narrowbody base.

Inside Project Winton, a name drawn from Winton, Queensland, where Qantas was founded in 1920, the airline is pairing A321XLRs at the mainline level with Airbus A220s, including A220-300s, for QantasLink to modernize its narrowbody operations across different route tiers. Unlike most other operators that use the A321XLR purely as a long-range specialty jet, Qantas is aligning its capacity growth with how demand behaves across both major domestic city pairs and thinner regional or international links.

Passenger volume and financial upside sit right at the center of that calculus. The reality for Qantas is that the 737 fleet carries nearly half of all passengers the airline flies each year, so upgrading that core segment of the fleet directly affects everyday schedule reliability, seat capacity, and unit economics across high-frequency domestic flying. Replacing 737-800s with A321XLRs and A220-300s is also projected to add between AUD 150 million and AUD 200 million per year to earnings by 2027, as reported by Simple Flying, which gives Qantas a clear financial incentive to push forward with the transition even when many XLRs fly domestic sectors.

Range and route versatility add another layer to how Qantas weighs the decision. While the A321XLR offers up to 5,400 miles (8,700 km) of range, roughly 1,864 miles (3,000 km) farther than the 737, Qantas does not need to fly every single A321XLR at maximum range to get value out of the airframe. Having extra range and cabin capacity in reserve lets the airline deploy the same aircraft type across busy domestic trunks and keep the option open for longer domestic sectors and selected regional international routes as demand warrants.

Uncover how Qantas' A321XLR is set to revolutionize Australian air travel, with the potential to open up new routes to Southeast Asia and beyond.

From Qantas' perspective, the A321XLR is about network flexibility and opening markets that current narrowbodies cannot serve reliably. Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson has emphasized that the extra-long-range narrowbody gives the airline flexibility to reach destinations its current narrowbody fleet cannot, pairing domestic workhorse duties with international options such as the scheduled Brisbane–Manila service, as noted by Airliner World. For an airline operating across vast Australian distances and regional Asian markets, having range in reserve lets Qantas adapt schedules, no longer having to commit widebodies to thinner routes.

Outside observers, however, read the aircraft's role in different ways, some with enthusiasm and others with skepticism. Enthusiasts and frequent-flyer commentators, including voices on One Mile At A Time and r/QantasAirways, often view the A321XLR as a practical, high-capacity narrowbody alternative that upgrades single-aisle comfort and capacity on busy domestic and regional hops. By contrast, Analytic Flying has floated a different theory suggesting cargo capability played a role in the selection, an argument that remains speculative rather than Qantas' stated rationale, especially because adding a Rear Center Tank for extra fuel reduces underfloor cargo volume compared with a standard A321neo.

Those differing viewpoints highlight why the A321XLR has drawn so much attention in aviation circles. Qantas is treating long-range capability as a strategic buffer for route flexibility and network growth, whereas outside analysts test every angle of the economics, from payload and fuel-tank trade-offs to whether a domestic-heavy fleet needs extra range on every flight.

Choosing the Airbus A321XLR over other narrowbody and cabin options comes down to how Qantas manages seat density, onboard comfort, and range headroom with a range of different flying profiles. Selecting an extended-range Airbus narrowbody over a standard 737-sized replacement, like the MAX, gives Qantas a single airframe family with higher passenger capacity and longer-sector reach than a baseline 737-800, meaning that capacity can be properly matched on a route-by-route basis.

Inside the A321XLR subfleet itself, Qantas is splitting cabin layouts rather than forcing one interior onto every flight. Early domestic-configured A321XLRs pack 197 or 200 seats, including 20 recliner business seats, to maximize capacity on high-demand routes, while 16 A321XLRs scheduled from 2028 introduce lie-flat business suites with sliding doors and 19-inch (48 cm) screens for longer domestic and international sectors.

Contrasting domestic trunk flying against pure long-haul deployment also shows why Qantas' approach stands apart from airlines using the A321XLR mainly for thin international routes. Across the industry, the overall consensus, as noted by Cirium, is to reserve the XLR for distant international routes, but Qantas flies most of them on busy domestic routes, keeping range in reserve for longer domestic and international sectors. That trade-off means domestic flyers on early XLRs get recliner seats rather than lie-flat beds, making route-matched tiering central to the strategy.

The story of the Qantas 737 is coming to an end, and with that, many pilots will be left without an aircraft to fly. What will the airline do?

Replacing all of the 737-800s with A321XLRs is not an overnight swap or a risk-free transition, and several caveats and operational risks shape how the fleet shift unfolds on the ground. 737-800 retirements are rolling out gradually rather than all at once, under Qantas' seven-year sale agreement covering 44 737-800s and 88 CFM56-7B engines with aftermarket specialist AerFin, initial exits are starting in late 2026 with 9 more planned for 2027, and select remaining 737-800s are slated for cabin refurbishments from 2027 to keep older frames competitive during the multi-year handover.

Cabin layout adjustments and route schedule shifts also test how quickly the new narrowbody settles into everyday service. As reported by Simple Flying, early A321XLR deliveries drew scrutiny over economy washroom ratios before Qantas added a third economy lavatory, trimming seat count by 3 seats from the fourth aircraft onward and planning retrofits for the earliest jets. Additionally, the A321XLR's international debut on Brisbane–Manila shifted from October 25, 2026, to February 1, 2027, leaving Airbus A330-200s on the route in the meantime.

Finally, delivery timing and supply-chain exposure are still very real variables for Qantas' fleet planners. Because Qantas built flexibility into its retirement schedule in case A321XLR deliveries slip, any ongoing manufacturing or supply-chain bottlenecks could keep older 737-800s, or interim widebody assignments, in service longer than initially hoped, making disciplined delivery progression essential as the transition begins to mature.

The bottom line is straightforward because Qantas is genuinely replacing its 737-800s with the A321XLR, using a long-range narrowbody primarily to support its high-demand domestic flying while still keeping extra range in reserve for longer domestic and international routes. For Qantas, the A321XLR is not an all-or-nothing long-haul specialist, and is adapting the jet to Australia's busiest single-aisle corridors and pacing the transition over several years.

For passengers and industry watchers alike, what matters next is how smoothly deliveries, cabin configurations, and route schedules come together across the late 2020s and how that will affect the airline's plans. With initial 737-800 exits underway, the Brisbane–Manila A321XLR launch set for February 1, 2027, and lie-flat business suite frames scheduled to arrive from 2028, Qantas' narrowbody fleet will look quite a lot different by the end of the decade, even as some 737-800s still remain part of the picture along the way.

The 737's will be flying late in to the 2030's, maybe even the early 2040's.

I suspect QF's retirement plan isn't based on fuel efficiency or type of aircraft, but capacity and underlying demand for the routes it flies. As such, the A220, B737 & A321XLR strategy may not only be revenue positive, but a lot more economical than the previous all 737 fleet.

For me, the question revolves around complexity and if having three different aircraft types for what will be a relatively small airline fleet going to be economically and operationally advantages. Think of three different lots of spare parts, maintenance personnel, flight crews and supporting infrastructure.

Replacing inferior product with a new thinking of premium cabin and long range with every narrowbody flight only gives them more flexibility to design their route network.

Citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

It has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

Citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

Like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

Generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points

Unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

Even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a big benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

Read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

In many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT."

If a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

Citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

#6117. How Much Does It Cost To Fly A Private Jet From New York To California?

Private jet travel has boomed in popularity since the pandemic, as more people found out how flexible and convenient it was. The time saved at airports is considerable, with all the processes streamlined, efficient, and personalized. Private jets are luxurious and very comfortable, as well as saving precious time.

As such, for high-flying business executives, celebrities, or ultra-high-net-worth individuals, flying privately offers the best experience, especially in the United States, where business jets are a firm feature. Private jet travel can be expensive, but how much does it cost to travel from New York to California?

One of the most popular destinations for private jets is Los Angeles, so let's use that as a guideline and look at some different options. Is there a cheaper way to fly private? Is it cheaper to consider private ownership or charter with an operator on a regular basis? Let's find out!

In this case, Teterboro Airport (KTEB) in New Jersey is an ideal airport for New York as it is dedicated to business jets and is just 12 miles away from Manhattan. The airport is well-supported with five FBOs available. Van Nuys Airport (KVNY) is the airport of choice for Los Angeles. It is 20 minutes from downtown. The airport sees more than 260,000 movements per year and is one of the busiest private aviation airports in the world.

According to Air Charter Advisors, chartering a private jet from New York to Los Angeles can start at around $40,000 for a one-way flight on a Cessna Citation Longitude or $50,000 for a heavy jet such as the Bombardier Challenger 604 or Dassault Falcon 2000LXS. Stratos Jets recommends the Bombardier Challenger 300 for this particular trip and estimates a cost of between $34,000 and $41,000 for a one-way flight.

Clay Lacy suggests that a round trip from New York to Los Angeles on a Gulfstream G450 may cost $102,000, and prices include the aircraft, crew, and fuel. Not included in the price are positioning flight time, landing fees, federal excise taxes, or overnight fees. A trip on a light jet between the two cities could cost $56,000, and $79,000 on a mid-size jet.

Discover private jet charter costs worldwide, top aircraft choices, and leading companies. Fly private with flexibility and luxury!

Larger and more luxurious jets with more range will command much higher hourly rates than something like a Pilatus PC-12. Of course, the longer the flight, the more fuel is used, and the crew will accrue more hours, adding more to the overall cost. The flight time between New York and LA is typically between five and a half and six and a half hours, depending on the aircraft type.

Private jets are chartered by the hour and can range from $3,500 up to $18,000 per hour. The price varies depending on the type of private jet and its size, as well as many other factors. According to Evojets, the 'ballpark' prices for chartering a private jet and their hourly rate are detailed in the table below.

Traveling at peak times or during the holidays can also influence the cost of chartering a private jet. If the aircraft needs to be repositioned to pick up the passengers or to return to base, this can result in additional costs. There may also be costs for landing fees or permits, and fuel costs can fluctuate, leading to surcharges. Other extra costs may include crew salary and per diem, accommodation and ground transport costs, and catering.

If money is no object, it is an easy process.

Looking at private ownership and operating costs, a pre-owned Gulfstream IV, for example, can be bought for around $3.2 million for an early 1990s model (production ceased in 1992), according to Liberty Jet. The budget needed per year for 200 hours would be $1,668,667. Taking into account the cost of fuel and the aircraft's speed, it equates to an average cost per mile of $19.12.

If the shortest distance in the air between New York and Los Angeles is 2,446 miles (via a distance calculator), in this case, the flight (one way) would cost $46,767.52 to operate on a Gulfstream IV that flies 200 hours a year. This does not include the initial aircraft cost, just the operating costs, fixed and variable.

Furthermore, Guardian Jet figures are based on 300 operating hours per year, annual fixed costs of $1,070,534, and variable hourly costs of $6,870.20 per hour, meaning that the flight could cost around $62,630. Of course, with private ownership, there are many variables in the equation.

As such, these figures are only estimated based on the given information and should not be considered fully accurate. There are other alternatives to both private ownership and charter: it all depends on the individual and how much they fly.

Because a single private flight can cost anything from a few thousand dollars to well over six figures, it is imperative that fliers prep ahead.

​​​One option is fractional ownership, where you can buy shares in an aircraft. There are usually 16 shares in an aircraft, and they are based on 800 flying hours a year. Therefore, you can buy 1/16th of an aircraft and acquire 50 flying hours, or 2/16ths for 100 hours, and so on. The cost will vary depending on the aircrafttype. On top of that, there are usually monthly management fees and an occupied hourly fee. All fees are fixed in advance.

A jet card or membership plan is another option. It works like a pre-paid card, where your flying hours are bought in advance and then used when needed. These are fixed hourly rates that are agreed upon in advance with a broker or operator. Of course, with these and fractional ownership, you have an aircraft at your disposal, without all the costs and hassles of ownership and paying for crew, insurance, hangar, and everything else.

Empty legs can offer another cheaper alternative to charter. These are when an aircraft is repositioned to return to base without passengers or flying empty to meet passengers somewhere else. Some charter companies will sell these at a highly discounted rate, as much as 50%, 75%, or even 90%, in order to recoup some of the costs. A search on Fly Victor showed that empty legs between New York and Los Angeles could be found for the costs detailed in the table above.

One of the cheapest ways to take advantage of the private aviation industry.

To get an accurate quote for a trip between New York and Los Angeles, a client should contact a few different charter operators or brokers to compare. It is important to have specific dates in mind, the number of passengers traveling, and any special requirements.

This can include catering, special amenities, or celebrating a special occasion. The more details, the better. A charter operator or broker will use this information to calculate the cost, which can vary based on factors like aircraft availability, fuel costs, airport fees, and the duration of your trip.

Each quote will be tailored to the client's exacting needs, based on the aircraft that are available and the current market conditions. If the client travels frequently by private jet, then private ownership is a possibility, but fractional ownership, jet cards, and memberships are also useful to avoid the extra costs and hassles of ownership. Empty legs are a more affordable alternative for a simple one-way charter at a discounted price.

When flying regularly between New York and Los Angeles, there are lots of options and varying prices, so it is important to check and compare for the most competitive price. It is always a good idea to get a few quotes from different brokers and not settle on the first price, unless the client is traveling in an emergency at the last minute.

#6116. Millions could lose paid benefits due to Congress ignoring decades of Social Security warnings: experts

Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, and Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, warned that Congress’ 50 years of action have led Social Security to the cliff of insolvency.

A panel filled with top economists, including a Nobel Peace Prize winner, warned Congress decades ago that its reforms to Social Security could spell disaster.

Now, experts tell Fox News Digital that the group from a bygone era was right as the safety net program hurtles toward a crisis that could affect millions.

"Social Security benefits were put on autopilot back in 1977," Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow of the American Enterprise Institute, told Fox News Digital. "Since then, Congress has done as little as it possibly could."

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled a report on the decades-old program that blasted it as a "Ponzi scheme" and warned that Social Security’s slide into insolvency began in the 1970s, when, despite warnings, lawmakers opted to tie benefit growth to wages rather than inflation.

AMERICANS MISLED ON SOCIAL SECURITY FOR DECADES AS CLOCK COUNTS DOWN ON BENEFITS, EXPLOSIVE REPORT REVEALS

President Jimmy Carter shakes hands with Louisiana Sen. Russell Long after signing the Social Security bill at the White House in Washington on Dec. 20, 1977. (Getty Archive)

Johnson wrote in his report that, at the time, an expert panel was formed that warned lawmakers that if they were to tie benefits to inflation, "Social Security would likely be sustainable today."

Still, lawmakers at the time ran with their own amendments to the program, which were signed into law by former President Jimmy Carter in December 1977.

"What they said in 1977 was if you index benefit growth to wages, you're effectively building a solvency crisis into the program," Biggs said. "You are over-promising, you're going to build in benefits that the current system can't afford to pay and you're committing future taxpayers to pay rates of taxes that the taxpayers in 1977 weren't willing to pay."

In the decades since, Congress has done little to change the program.

SENATE REPUBLICANS BREAK THROUGH WASHINGTON GRIDLOCK WITH MASSIVE AMERICAN ENERGY, DATA CENTER OVERHAUL

Romina Boccia, the Cato Institute’s director of budget and entitlement policy, told Fox News Digital that’s largely because lawmakers have not had the political will to do it.

She agreed with Johnson that Social Security was effectively a "Ponzi scheme," and said "there's this misconception that a lot of Americans think that Social Security is a retirement savings program."

"But for that, you would actually need to have savings occur in the system, and there would need to be assets that would be invested in earning returns," Boccia said. "That's not the case. We're talking about a pay-as-you-go program."

One of the side effects of Congress’ lack of action to rein in the program is that the wage growth formula relies on workers in the economy contributing with their paychecks.

Boccia noted that as the decades have gone on, "we've seen a severe decline in the number of workers compared to the number of retirees collecting benefits as a result of a decline in fertility."

DEMOCRATS COULD ENTER CONGRESSIONAL MAJORITY IN A GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., makes his way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Sept. 30, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Congress’ last real successful effort to reform Social Security came in the early 1980s, Biggs noted, when lawmakers were forced to step in to deal with the "funding crisis" hitting the program.

"They raised taxes. They increased the retirement age. So, they did this with months to spare to fix Social Security," Biggs said. "It's not something they wanted to do, but they were forced to do.

"Now, in 2032, we're going to face the same situation, where Congress will be forced to take action sometime before the trust fund runs out in 2032, not because they want to, but because they're forced to do it," he continued.

If Social Security’s trust fund runs dry by 2032, Americans’ benefits would be slashed, and the onus of paying for the shortfall would add trillions more to the nation’s debt.

But Johnson, in his report, declared that the Social Security problem could not be fixed between now and then because of Congress’ inaction for the last several decades. And he suggested the solution would be to repeal a possible benefits reduction as the program’s trust fund heads toward insolvency in just under seven years.

Biggs, who was part of former President George W. Bush’s effort to reform Social Security over two decades ago, said that, had Congress taken action "25 years ago, you could fix Social Security in barely noticeable ways."

"There is no easy fix to Social Security today, and that stems entirely from the fact that, every year, when Congress has had the opportunity to fix Social Security, they chose to duck the issue for political reasons and kick the can down the road," Biggs said.

Boccia disagreed with Johnson’s solution and contended that the real answer was one that lawmakers of yesterday and today would be hesitant to approach — raising taxes.

"The real way to think about this is that there's almost no way to imagine Congress would let those benefit cuts take effect," Boccia said. "It will be so politically toxic. So, most likely they're going to try to find a different solution.

"The last time the trust fund was running out of money in 1982, Congress put together a commission and then voted on a bill that increased taxes and reduced benefits, including raising the social security retirement age," she continued.

"The problem is that the funding gap now is much larger, more than two times bigger than it was in the ‘80s."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

#6115. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

Washingtonians have a new option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a new thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the new IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

The new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United plans to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows.

IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

The state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate plans to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx said in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.
